speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF MEMBERS OF U.S. CONGRESS
speechtext:
From time immemorial it has been a convention in accordance with British parliamentary tradition that no one is permitted within the precincts of the House of Commons except the members, the reason being, as Your Honour knows, that in the days of Charles I and prior thereto, if there was anyone of distinction or power present in the gallery the freedom of members of parliament to speak was, to say the least, circumscribed if not denied. That tradition survives today in the fiction that there is no one present at any time in the galleries of the House of Commons.
Nevertheless, these fears of intimidation on this occasion, however distinguished the delegation, do not prevent me-and I hope the house will not deny me-the privilege and opportunity of welcoming the members of the United States Senate and House of Representatives who are in this city meeting with the parliamentary representatives of Canada. The agenda is an important one dealing with such matters as foreign affairs, defence, and economic problems which activate each of our nations. The relationship between our countries, long one of the closest in the world, is represented officially by such organizations as the international joint commission and the permanent joint board on defence and, on the cabinet level by the committee on joint defence and the committee on trade and economic questions.
These members of the United States congress who are with us today bring to us the strength, the vigour and the knowledge of the co-operation which prevails between our two countries. I for one, many years ago, advocated in this chamber the need of bringing together representatives of the United States and Canada, and I was joined in that opinion by the hon. member for
Laurier. In the intervening years those meetings were not achieved, except through the parliamentary group of the commonwealth parliamentary association, until 1958. Since then there have been these exchanges between parliamentarians of our countries which mean so much to each of us, joined together not only geographically but in the mind and soul for the maintenance and preservation of freedom.
Our interdependence cannot be achieved without mutual awareness. There will be problems. There have been problems. We solve them through the instrumentality of discussion and agreement. The removal of misunderstandings is a continuing task with us. We do this in the broad and harmonious perspective of understanding. Unofficial though this organization is, it has already contributed much to understanding between oui countries and the solution of problems which have risen, and I know that that function will continue in the years ahead.
It is therefore my privilege as Prime Minister, through you, sir, to extend to Senatoi Aiken as chairman of the visiting group o: senators and congressmen the thanks of the Canadian parliament for their visit with us, coupled with the warmest welcome that we can accord to those with whom we are united in sentiment and dedication.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF MEMBERS OF U.S. CONGRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me very special pleasure to join with the Prime Minister on behalf of the official opposition in the welcome he has extended to our guests from the United States. To adapt that expression of the seventeenth century which the Prime Minister mentioned as one inspiring intimidation, we might say in this case "We spy friends".
This joint committee of the United States congress and the Canadian parliament is, as the Prime Minister has said, playing an increasingly useful part in examining into and strengthening the good relations between our two countries, helping to keep the neighbourhood fences in good repair, a result that does not just happen of itself.
In Canada, relations with our neighbour have been a major concern of ours ever since we became a nation, and indeed before that. The problems arising out of those relations are nothing new; yet we have always, at least in this century, managed to settle our difficulties in a manner which reflects the

Congress Members in Gallery genuine friendship and underlying good will between our two peoples. Perhaps it is well to recall this at this time in order to keep problems in perspective and to remind ourselves of the deeper and more important things that bind us together in a dangerous world.
Senator Aiken, who is a member of the United States delegation and whom we all know, respect and admire, said the other day that the United States and Canada cannot differ too much because our interests are "hopelessly interlocked". They are also, I believe, "hopefully" interlocked. Co-operation between us in defence, in trade and in everything else is essential. There will be honest differences among us in Canada as to the best methods for achieving co-operation in a changing world, but there will be no differences between us as to the necessity for such co-operation and the necessity for working together in an effort to promote progress, peace and security in the world today with justice and freedom for all.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF MEMBERS OF U.S. CONGRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join with the Prime Minister and Leader of the Opposition in welcoming to our galleries the distinguished representatives from the United States Senate and House of Representatives. In the past I have had the good fortune of being a member of the Canadian part of this joint interparliamentary group, and I can say that in those initial discussions I believe we had a frank exchange of views. I believe that the establishment of this group can and should lead to a better understanding between our nations.
It would not be frank on my part, Mr. Speaker, if I did not say that in view of the C.C.F.-New Party there are major outstanding differences between our two nations with regard to trade, economic, defence and other problems; but we are convinced that with clear and frank discussion, with an honest effort to settle those differences, we can make progress in building democracy, freedom and prosperity.
Our rules are not the same-we find that out every day-as the rules governing debate in the United States congress. Under our rules we are not able to give the same kind of extended welcome that some of us have received on the floor of the United States Senate; none the less, under our procedures where we have party representation, we can say to our distinguished friends that they receive today a unanimous welcome from the Canadian House of Commons.

subtopic: CANADIAN DELEGATION TO RESUMED GENERAL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish now to announce the composition of the Canadian delegation to the resumed session of the United Nations general assembly on March 7. The Canadian delegation will be led, of course, by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green). The vice-chairman will be the parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt). The remaining delegates and alternate delegates will be drawn

entirely from the group who served during the first half of the general assembly session last fall. Arrangements are being made for parliamentary observers to attend. While I am unable at the moment to give their names, they will be drawn, as usual, two from this side of the house and one from each of the opposition parties.
The delegation will be slightly smaller than for a regular session because the assembly disposed of a major portion of its business before it recessed at Christmas. Three of the assembly's main committees have already completed their work, and the delegation to the resumed session is to deal with the work of the remaining four committees.
The delegation will in fact consist of Senator Blois from the other place, the hon. member for Calgary South, the hon. member for Charlevoix and, from the Department of External Affairs, General Burns, the government's disarmament adviser, Mr. C. S. A. Ritchie, the Canadian permanent representative to the United Nations, and Mr. Morley Scott.
The Canadian government for its part hopes that the renewed debates may serve to improve the international atmosphere and that progress will be made particularly on the problem of disarmament.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR PROTEST AGAINST POLITICAL MURDERS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REQUEST FOR PROTEST AGAINST POLITICAL MURDERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Would the minister care to comment on the reported continuation of political murders in the Congo? Will Canada speak out strongly against this revolting blood bath?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: REQUEST FOR PROTEST AGAINST POLITICAL MURDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt whatever about the revulsion felt in Canada generally, by all members of this house and also, I suggest, in every country of the world, at the continuing reports of assassinations for political purposes in the Congo. It is precisely to put an end to this and other acts of bloodshed in the Congo that the latest security council resolution gives greater authority for the United Nations to intervene in the Congolese situation.
It is too early yet to have arrived at a precise assessment or interpretation of all the implications of the security council resolution of February 21. Various measures calling for procedures of implementation have been included in the resolution. These measures are broad in scope, and it has not yet been established in what way the United Nations will carry them out. Various Congolese leaders are known to have taken strong exception to one or more of the measures envisaged in the resolution.
However, as the most important purpose of the security council resolution is to prevent civil war in the Congo, it can be assumed that the United Nations representatives will rely

Inquiries of the Ministry primarily on consultation, persuasion and conciliation to bring about co-operation among the various factions and with the United Nations forces on the ground. This would appear to offer the best hope of pacification and stabilization in the Congo.
I suggest that at this date we should not be concentrating our attention on this question of the possible use of force. The resolution states clearly that force would be used only if necessary and in the last resort. I am sure that we can rely on the good judgment of the Irish commander of the U.N. forces in the Congo, General McKeown, to act responsibly.
I would point out again that as the purpose of the United Nations is to prevent civil war, its immediate recourse must surely be to the arts of peace, namely patient negotiation and conciliation.

Mr. Speaker, I noted with interest the press release issued by Mr. Larry Sefton, director district 6, united steel workers of America, charging intimidation of unemployed workers by officials of the national employment service at Galt. This indeed is a reflection upon the national employment service, the hon. member for Waterloo South, and myself since, I, too was mentioned in this press release. This reference also appeared in the newspaper article to which the hon. member referred.
In essence, Mr. Sefton takes exception to the fact that persons who had forwarded printed cards to the hon. member for Waterloo South were called into the office of the unemployment insurance commission and interviewed with a view to finding employment for them. He also charges that they were reprimanded for sending cards to the hon. member.
My office has been in touch with Mr. Fitz-gibbon, the manager of the Galt office, and we are assured that no person interviewed was reprimanded or criticized in any way for having signed the cards in question. What happened was that on receipt of a number

of cards which were forwarded in line with what Mr. Sefton describes as-and I quote the report in part-"a postcard campaign for jobs" and which cards read, in part:

This is normal procedure and something that is done in every case when any individual writes indicating that he or she is without employment.
The necessary follow-up to such procedure is, of course, to bring the individual in for interview with a view to determining his employability and his availability for work. I might say in this connection that while the national placement service are operating in an efficient manner, they have not yet reached the point where they are in a position to refer people to jobs without interviewing them.
The interviews in question, conducted in accordance with the accepted practices for such interviews and in a genuine spirit of attempting to find work for the persons involved, turned up some interesting facts. Perhaps the facts that became evident might account for Mr. Sefton's objection to having such persons interviewed at all.

I wish to make one other general observation and two particular observations. I am interested in many other matters but they can be suitably ventilated before the committee. May I say I was most gratified in examining the estimates of the minister to see what a substantial amount is being devoted to the education of the Indians. I think this was emphasized in the statement of the minister when she devoted at least half the time taken in presenting her statement to the question of education. I think this is most essential and important, because it is at that level that we are going to be able to do something. However, I might point out that if possible we should do even more than we are doing now, not only because of the humanitarian principles involved, not only because we have a duty to undo some of the neglect which has been the lot of the Indians in the past, a neglect which in recent years, I am happy to say, has certainly been dealt with more than adequately. Those are ample motives in themselves, but there is another reason I should like to mention which may be of some assistance to the minister when she is asking for those funds which are essential for the discharge of her responsibilities.
This country has a pre-eminent position among the small and middle siz;e nations of the world today. One reason for that is undoubtedly that the ugly head of racial and colour bias and prejudice has not been observed in Canada. Unfortunately too many other leading countries in the western world are not in that position. In recent days there has been an appalling and atrocious series of riots involving bloodshed which have swept through the world and indicate the possibility of warfare on the basis of race and colour. In the face of this situation I think it is most important for us to remember that in part we occupy the position we do because of the regard which other nations of the world have for us in this respect. If anything, this should be an invitation to the minister to be even more zealous and indefatigable in dealing with this problem, and the same thing applies to her officials. The situation is one where time is not on our side; and in commending the attitude of the department I hope they will have that in mind and that their efforts will be increased even more.

I wish to mention one more point having to do particularly with the question of education in my own area. I have been in touch with the minister and her officials about the matter and have been adequately satisfied as to their appreciation of the problem, but I think I should put my views on record in a general way.
In the northern part of my constituency there are several thousand Indians who until recently lived in a nomadic state in which they engaged in trapping, hunting and fishing. Only in the last generation can it be said that they have come nearer to the settlements in the north such as Fort Vermilion, Harbay and Assumption. In pursuit of the desire to see that these Indians receive an adequate education, arrangements have been made from time to time to take students in the higher grades to Edmonton, Calgary and other larger centres. It is my belief that in some cases a period of transition should elapse before these Indian boys and girls are considered to be adequately equipped to absorb the white culture which is found in the larger centres. I feel that at least for one more generation many of these boys and girls might well fit into the pattern of integration in an area closer to their own homes, where I think the results to be achieved will be more apparent.
I was glad to hear the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River say the other day that he had finally been able to consummate his request for a dormitory and hostel in connection with a residential school. I am glad to move into the vacant room which he has iust left. I would urge the department officials to give some consideration to a similar type of accommodation in the Fort Vermilion irea. I have been in touch with them as I say, md I have had the satisfaction of receiving acknowledgment from them that they are aware of the problem. But may I say that I lonestly and sincerely believe that it may ''et be some time before these young boys md girls are adequately equipped to receive and benefit from the education they will atherwise be getting in places like Edmonton.

The minister indicated earlier, in connection with forestry, that co-operation with the provincial authorities was necessary on forest surveys. How much of the money, $50,000 last year and $17,000 this year, has gone to the provincial governments for services in connection with surveys, or has this survey money been spent by the minister's own forestry officers? If so, I would be rather staggered by that amount of money.

I think the hon. member misunderstood me. I said that our own new Department of Forestry was undertaking surveys for us. The reason for the reduction from $50,000 to $17,000 is that the work which was formerly done for us by the provincial government of British Columbia and other outside agencies is now being done by our own staff. Consequently this expenditure was reduced considerably.

Could the minister say, in general terms-let us say, in silviculture terms -what we got for that $50,000 expenditure on surveys. Were these just surveys to develop forestry maps of the areas, or did they extend further into survey plans for roads, logging possibilities and this type of thing?

I have not the figures broken down completely, but most of this work was carried out in British Columbia. It was largely for the purpose of establishing just what was available in the respective areas.

Has the minister any indication of what is going to be spent in Ontario? The minister gave statistics in the house previously on the number of square miles of forested areas on reserves in Ontario, and they were considerable.
This whole question of forestry and forest reserves has been opened up by the government, not only with the creation of the Department of Forestry but in all the plans announced by the Minister of Agriculture. I feel that forestry in all its aspects could
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration be one of the most important means of livelihood for Indians in Ontario. Perhaps the minister could indicate how the policy has been directed to fit in with these other developments.

While we are looking to see if we have the figures for Ontario for last year I might tell the hon. member that the $17,000 which is in the estimates this year comprises $10,000 for forest surveys and $7,000 for reforestation. This covers all provinces. I have not the figures broken down here.

That is a very minor sum for reforestation. I would hope that in future that would go up. I can understand our not spending money now, in view of the legislation which is pending that may encourage other people to spend this money.
I wonder whether we are now going to have a forestry section within the branch; and if it is expanding, what plans are under way to see that at the technical level young Indians are being trained in the forestry field? We have a school of forestry for people at the technical level, the scaler or cruiser level, at the lakehead; there is another such school in New Brunswick and I believe there is at least one in British Columbia.
I wonder whether any young Indians are being trained in these schools to work in this field, or are they merely being used for axe-men, and that type of thing, in forestry planning?

We have some Indians in training in fire fighting, but the staff engaged in forestry at the present time consists of two foresters and provision for a third. They are under the reserves and trust division of the department. I think it would be safe to say that as time goes on and as the work is developed we will certainly train Indians, if we can find Indians who are capable of doing the work which is required of them with the appropriate training.

The reason I raise the point is that we notice that a great many Indians are taking courses in nursing and teaching, and they come back to work with their own people. Surely forestry would be one of the best fields for them.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to get a clearer picture with respect to the supervisory and administrative power in relation to certain phases of Indian affairs. Who would make the decision with respect to a survey of timber reserves on Indian land? Who would decide whether or not the timber should be sold? Who makes decisions as to hunting and trapping rights on Indian lands? In a situation where the Indians cannot sell timber or hunt and trap and where the Indians are faced with hunger, who would initiate action and on what basis would the Indians be taken care of? I could illustrate my question by reading an article which appears in today's Ottawa Citizen:
Indian chief says Tories broke word.
A Manitoba Indian chief told an Indian-Metis conference Wednesday that a number of the 2,000 Indians on his island lake reserve have come to him to ask what they could eat this winter.
Chief Alfred McDougall, speaking in Cree through an interpreter, said the federal government has broken promise after promise.
The government, he charged, has refused to allow Indians to sell timber from their land and has watched without acting while the Indian's main source of livelihood-trapping and hunting-dwindled away.
Chief McDougall said he has been trying for three years to get the federal government to do something about the forest reserves on the Indian land.
This ties in with complaints we continuously hear. Who makes decisions with respect to the welfare of Indians and the utilization of resources on their reserves?

In the first instance a request for action comes from the band council. It is not at all unusual that an individual on a reservation will have a difference of opinion with the council of his band. Sometimes we have formal resolutions from band councils and private letters from individuals which are completely at variance.

Who has the authority, the band or the chief?

In the first place the band would probably pass a resolution which would then be forwarded to the department. Certain deliberations or investigations would take place, as the case might be, depending on the type of problem that is involved. It is the duty of the officials of the department to see that the Indians are properly taken care of and that their resources are preserved wherever possible.

Mr. Chairman, I have a question I should like to put to the minister, prompted by the questions asked by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. I remember some years ago there was a good deal of trouble about provincial roads which went through Indian reserves. I am not talking about proposed roads where there was not a right of way but of cases where rights of way already existed and there were roads of a sort.
My recollection is that the view that was taken at one time was that if this was a provincial highway the provincial government would have to make some contribution to it and the federal government would not simply build the highway through the reserve. I think that policy was somewhat relaxed in one or two cases.
I wonder if the minister could say what the general policy is now with respect to provincial highways that pass through Indian reserves. Who has the responsibility for their upkeep and what contribution does the federal government make? Could the minister say whether there are any outstanding problems in this field?

Generally speaking, Mr. Chairman, if it is a provincial highway the responsibility lies with the province for its maintenance. As the hon. member knows there


may be extenuating circumstances in certain areas where the road is not heavily travelled by the non-Indian community. As the hon. member knows, we have one area where the trans-Canada highway goes right through a reservation. In that instance I believe the land was purchased outright and of course the highway is the responsibility of the federal government.
The situation varies in different locations depending on the extent to which the road is valuable to the Indians on the reserve and the extent to which it is valuable to the non-Indians who seek to go through Indian lands to arrive at their destination.
At the present moment I cannot think of any particularly troublesome areas apart from the one enunciated by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, which has been a sore point for a long time. Other than that, I cannot recall any that are real problems at the moment.

Would the hon. lady bring me up to date on Pointe Bleue and the Indian reserve across the river from Three Rivers in Nicolet county, I think, although I am not sure of that. There was also a situation in Saskatchewan somewhere in the constituency of the Minister of Agriculture, about which I recall something. No doubt the officials will remember all of these very well.
The hon. member is speaking of the road problems only?
Yes, in those three places.
Mr. Chairman, so far as we know, the problems in both cases have been solved.
There were three.

In Saskatchewan, we have an agreement with the province on what is known as the grid road system under which the federal government and the province contribute on a fifty-fifty basis. With respect to Pointe Bleue, we have in the current estimates an allotment of $5,000 for the construction of approximately 600 feet of street in the new welfare housing site and $15,000 for the construction of approximately four miles of new road, including widening, ditching and installation of culverts.

What about the reserve in Nicolet county?

Very well.
And also who paid for whatever may have been done.
I will give the hon. member a report.

It was alleged very strongly in the Ontario legislature last year that Ontario hydro had

paid an exorbitant sum for the land that they bought from the Dimensional Company. The facts are all on Hansard for last year and it is not in dispute that land which was sold for about $2,000 an acre to Dimensional with the approval of the department appears to have been resold three days before the original sale, according to certain evidence that was put on Hansard and has never been contradicted to my knowledge, for $5,000 an acre more. It was on the basis of that position that I and one or two other members made the statement last year that either hydro had paid an utterly exorbitant sum for this land, a price which could not be defended, or the Indians had been gypped.
We know that a sufficiently serious view of this whole matter was taken by the premier of Ontario that he caused a royal commission to be appointed to inquire into the question of whether hydro had made an improper deal. That commission has reported, and I must say I have not read its report and do not intend to because that is not within our purview here. I have plenty to do reading those things that fall within the purview of parliament. However, judging from what the newspapers say, the commission reported that hydro had made a provident deal. I think some of us might still have some doubts about that but, as I say, that is not our business. It is the business of the members of the Ontario legislature and it is not our business. But I do say that if it is the case that hydro paid over $7,000 an acre for the land and made an agreement to pay three days before the sale to Dimensional was approved by the minister the Indians were gypped of about $5,000 an acre.
I do not want to suggest for one minute, any more than I did last year, that there was any wrongdoing on the part of the minister or the department but I do say that on the face of that evidence it is very hard not to feel that there was gross negligence, that the department should have taken the trouble to find out from hydro, which after all is a well known and presumably respectable body, what they were willing to pay for this property before a sale was made to a company which, judging from the evidence that was splashed all over the newspapers in Toronto and elsewhere at the time of the royal commission, was not one of the most ancient and reputable organizations in this country. I say that particularly in view of the fact that if the uncontradicted evidence that was put on Hansard is true, namely, that hydro agreed to make payment to this company three days before the federal agreement was made with Dimensional, then this does seem to me to be a really shocking way to treat a trust to the Indians.

I do not intend to spend a lot of time going into the details. I believe this matter ought to be inquired into not just by a provincial royal commission but by the federal government in order to find out whether or not this company already had an agreement with hydro on the basis of which it got a large part of its down payment before the agreement was ever concluded between the minister on behalf of the Indians and the Dimensional Company.
As I say, I think the whole sale was indefensible regardless of whether this hydro incident had occurred at all because I believe the price was not nearly high enough. I think that that valuable land, on which municipal taxes did not have to be paid as long as it was an Indian reservation, should at least never have been sold for less than the amount for which the previous government was willing to sell it. As I said last year and I repeat, I was very glad that the deal fell through because on second thought I felt it was inadvisable to sell at all. I think that land right on the edge of Sarnia, a city developing as that place is, should have been kept in trust in perpetuity for the Indians and that long term leases should have been made on a provident basis so that the Indians would have got the benefit of all this increment and not people like this Dimensional Company.
Whether or not it is true I do not know but I read in a very reputable newspaper the other day, the Globe and Mail, I think, that some mining company was now seeking to acquire a part of this land from Dimensional and, I feel fairly certain, not at the same price that only a year ago Dimensional paid to the Indians. I think this whole transaction was a highly improvident one for the government to have made. I think it would be a bad thing to do with land that was held in trust for all the people of Canada. But when you consider that this was a sale of a part of an Indian reserve held in trust for the Indians, and on the basis of what we know now, reinforced by this whitewashing report of the provincial royal commission,-if that is the right term to apply to it-it seems to me that if hydro made a provident deal, the minister made a most improvident one.

I cannot subscribe to that statement, Mr. Chairman. My hon. friend is rehashing a matter that was thoroughly discussed in the House of Commons last year. If he wants to make a statement to the effect that the Indians were cheated, then I make a statement to the effect that his remarks are decidedly irresponsible. The hon. member likes to talk about the deal which he proposed. His deal fell through. It turned out that the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration people with whom he was dealing did not have any money or it never reached the first stages.
Apparently they did not kpow Ontario Hydro.

They never saw fit to go through with the deal that was proposed. It never reached the first stages of fruition. To compare it with the one that was finalized and from which the Indians now have $2.5 million I think is to talk in an absolutely irresponsible way about a deal that has now been in effect for some time.
I might draw to his attention the fact that whatever happens subsequently to lands that are disposed of, that is a matter that scarcely comes under the jurisdiction of this department. When we were advising the Indians with respect to this particular deal, we were not satisfied with one valuation. We had three valuations and none of them came anywhere near the valuation that my hon. friend now likes to propose as being a true valuation for the property.
There are a great many things to be considered about this particular piece of land and its potential. I should like to put on record now the fact that we do not consider that any subsequent deal made by the company and hydro was necessarily one for the consideration of this department. We had no offer from hydro. We had an offer from this company. The offer from the company was for a large parcel of land. Hydro was interested in a relatively small portion of the land. Even if hydro had paid directly to the Indians at the same rate the amount they are reputed to have paid now, the Indians still would not have as much money as they have at the present time from this property.
As I said last year, Mr. Chairman-and I have no hesitation in saying it again-I think we made an excellent deal for the Indians and I have no apology to make to anybody, including the hon. member, for that deal.

I have not any apology to make either for what I have said. I did not make any valuation of this land. The Ontario hydro made the valuation of the land. The hon- lady agreed to sell and sold land or allowed to be sold land that belonged to the Indians for $2,000 an acre for which hydro subsequently paid $7,000 an acre; or rather, it was not subsequently because the evidence seems to be that they paid it three days before.
Can you prove it?

Hence it was a willing purchaser, and perhaps a too willing purchaser, that paid $5,000 an acre more than the hon. lady sold for, three days after the first agreement was made, according to the evidence.

If the hon. lady thinks it is none of her business, when her department knew that hydro was interested in this land, to enquire in advance whether they could not make a better deal with them, I regard that as a dereliction of duty and I do not think it is "irresponsible" for any member of parliament to describe it in those terms.
Then the hon. lady says they would not have received so much for the piece of land that hydro took as they have already received for a great deal more land than hydro took. Of course, that is true; but they would have had the rest of the land, something which is a rather important consideration.
If this reserve were up near James bay somewhere, there might be a great deal to be said for the view that it was needed for some special purpose that would exist for only one purchaser, that existed at only one point in time and that would enable the trustees for the Indians to sell at that time and reinvest the money in some other way that would be proper for the Indians. But anybody who has the slightest knowledge of what has gone on in the environs of Sarnia in the last 25 years knows that it is not a matter of speculation-although it appears to have been a matter of speculation in another sense of the term-but rather a matter of absolute certainty that unless we are going to have a deep Tory recession for a long time to come, this land is going to accelerate in value every year. If the government had to pay taxes on the land, if they had a large number of fixed charges they had to meet or if the Indians had been in desperate need of this money-as they were not-there might have been a much different situation. But there was no reason whatsoever for this precipitate, urgent sale except, apparently, the fact this Dimensional company came along and made an offer and managed, without the knowledge of the department, to sell a part of it in order to give them in advance, enough money with which to make their down payment. I say that this transaction, even apart from the hydro aspect of it, was an improvident one. But when one thinks of this hydro aspect which has now, as I say, been whitewashed by a royal commission in Ontario, one gets a different picture. Since the royal commission said that this land was worth $7,000 an acre, the hon. lady either repudiates the royal commission or she makes mincemeat of her sale at $2,000 an acre; and that is exactly what I am complaining about and what I say there is a proper complaint about with regard to those who have a special responsibility and special trust with regard to

these Indian lands. It seems to me that there was just a shocking neglect of the proper discharge of that trust.

Mr. Chairman, I repudiate that statement entirely. The hon. member knows full well that the land which was subsequently sold to hydro was not by any manner of means sold for $2,000 an acre. The figure of $2,000 an acre was the average price for the whole area and certainly not the price for the particular section of land which was sold to hydro.
I might draw something further to his attention. Since he seems to be so familiar with the proceedings of this royal commission, he had better read the part where the judge said he felt that the interests of the Indians had been well protected by this department.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I recognize the hon. member for York North who has been trying to get the floor for some time.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is being extremely unfair in his statement.
He always is unfair.

He states that he has not read this royal commission report and yet he says it was a whitewash. I think he made the same charges here last year with regard to the minister gypping the Indians. I say this to the hon. member: He has done it again and he has not investigated the report of the royal commission. If he had done so, he would not have made these statements he has made today. Another thing the hon. member did was to criticize the price. A large block of land was sold for $2,000 an acre. A small block-an extremely narrow block and a desirable one-was bought by the hydro at a higher price. What is wrong with that procedure? It is just another example of the great foresight of this group across the way, and it is similar to the stand they took the other day with regard to bonds that were sold and which they said should not have been sold. After three years they can see the difference. Frankly, Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member has been most unfair in his charges with regard to this matter.

I am glad I allowed the hon. member for York North to speak first because it is so much easier to reply. It
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration is none of our business what the royal commission says because the royal commission was investigating the conduct of a provincial body.
Why were you referring to it?
I was referring to it because, as the hon. gentleman knows very well, the royal commission said that what the hydro did was justified.
How do you know?

Because I read the newspapers, as the hon. member also does. I say, Mr. Chairman, it is reasonable to assume that when all three Toronto newspapers agree on a fact, it is likely to be a fact.
There does not seem to be much doubt that the royal commission did say this transaction was justified, that hydro was justified in paying $7,000 an acre. If that is so, that makes the case against the federal government that much worse. If the royal commission had said-as some people think it should have said-that this was a fixed deal and that hydro paid far too much, that would support the hon. lady. But if hydro paid a fair price at $7,000 an acre, then the hon. lady did not get a fair price at $2,000 an acre.
That is nonsense.

That is not nonsense at all. The hon. lady makes a great deal of fuss about this being a small area and the most desirable part. As a matter of fact the only evidence given, which the hon. lady has never attempted to deal with, is that this is about the most undesirable part of this tract of land because it happens to have, not one but I believe two of these hydro lines going across it. It would therefore not be a Suitable area for building.
Far from being the most valuable piece of land it is probably, except for hydro purposes, an almost useless piece of land according to the information about this particular tract, that has never been contradicted. The information I have about it may be wrong. I confess I have not gone down there myself and walked over it. I am not speaking from direct personal knowledge. But evidence was put on Hansard last year about these hydro lines going across this particular piece of land, about the purpose for which hydro wanted it and about its unsuitability for building purposes.
I will be very surprised if other tracts of this land are not resold by the present purchaser at an even higher price than hydro paid.
That is normal business.

Of course it is normal business; I am not criticizing the purchaser. But
2360	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration surely it is the duty of the government not to sell off Indian reserves, that are held in trust for the Indians, for less than their worth and for less than can be obtained for the benefit of the Indians, in order to enable a fly-bynight real estate operator to make a quick buck out of it.
We do not do that type of thing.
That is what you did.
Mr. Chairman, I do not know how many times I have to say this for it to sink in. Possibly it will never sink in.
He has a pretty tough hide.

We had three separate and distinct valuations of this property, taking into consideration not only present values but potential values in the area. The price received by the Indians for their land was a fair price. I cannot go any further than that. Every safeguard that could be taken was taken.
I am sure my hon. friend does not doubt my intentions in regard to the Indians. I have a very grave responsibility toward them. This deal was explained to them in detail; it was a deal they themselves wanted and accepted. I am sure that if my hon. friend, who talks about the fuss I made-and I might say this, he is the worst fussbudget in the house- would think back to his own experience in the department he would know that had this deal not gone through he would have reason to make an even bigger fuss.

I certainly would not. I accept the hon. lady's word about her intention; I have never at any time cast any reflection on her intentions. But I am dealing with facts, only with facts, and I intend to deal with facts.
I tell the committee this, and I hope no one doubts my word. I did agree to negotiate with a company in 1957. That company considered, until it found it impossible to finance the transaction, that this land-not quite as much, but nearly as much; nearly the same property [DOT]-was worth $8 million. The hon. lady sold it for $6-J million. If I had been minister, that fact alone would have given me plenty of reason for pausing, if between 1957 and 1960 the price offered for land-maybe they offered too much-
That is why they withdrew. They found they had offered too much.
The hon. lady is misrepresenting the facts. The hon. lady knows perfectly well that the arrangement for financing fell through-
That is a very nice excuse.

Whether it is an excuse or not, I am saying that if I had been in office and had been considering a transaction to sell Indian lands for $8 million, I would have looked long and hard before selling it for $6J million.
That is precisely what we did.

I would not have been satisfied with three valuations, knowing there was another potential purchaser for a part of that land and when, as it turned out, that potential purchaser was already in negotiation with the person to whom the hon. lady was making the sale to pay a price three and a half times as much as the hon. lady sold it for.
In the face of the facts it really does seem to be a transaction impossible to defend in any way.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a comment on this although I have come in late and I do not think I know all the facts. However, two or three things seem to me to be clear.
It seems to me this is a classic case that so often arises, of wisdom after the event. Anyone who has anything to do with business knows that real estate values often do strange things. I had a little experience myself. I sold a house for a figure which makes me blush now when I think of it. Why? Not because it was not a reasonable thing to do at the time, because I had the best opinions and it looked perfectly all right; but that house has since changed hands at figures I do not like to think of.
I do not blame anyone for that. Perhaps I blame myself a little, but I do not blame myself very much. Therefore when the minister tells us-and apparently this is not contradicted in any way-that there was not one valuation, not two valuations but three valuations, and presumably from reputable people, how it is possible to come along and say the matter was gone into hastily and in an ill-considered fashion passes my understanding.

I am sure that when the hon. member for Greenwood sold the house to which he referred he did not watch it change hands to another purchaser the next day, or even the day before, at a price three and a half times higher than he sold it for. That is what happened in this particular case.
The deal between hydro and Dimensional had, according to uncontradicted evidence that was put on Hansard last year-no one has yet attempted to contradict it-already

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
been made before the deal was made between Dimensional and the federal government.
It seems to me that is the most serious aspect of this matter. The department knew hydro wanted this land. The hon. lady admitted that before the hon. member for Greenwood came into the committee. They knew this land was wanted by hydro. Hydro is not like red China; surely it is recognized by the federal government as an entity to which they can speak. It surely should not have been very difficult for the hon. lady herself to pick up the telephone and ask Mr. McCauley or Mr. Duncan if they really wanted this property.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.
Is he saying that, against the wishes of the Indians who expressed themselves as not wishing to deal with hydro, I should have forced them to deal with hydro?

No, I am not saying any such thing. I am saying that the minister should not have agreed without exploring what hydro would pay and telling the Indians what hydro would pay. I am not saying the minister should have forced them to sell to hydro. I know she could not, according to law.
There is another aspect of this matter which I have not yet mentioned but which I will mention now. There was a meeting of the band council-the hon. lady knows about this because I asked questions about it earlier in the session-and just before the vote was taken the representative of the purchaser, a lawyer, went around and offered each of the Indians another $100. That was immediately before the vote was taken. This to me-

When was that?
was through and the vote had been taken this was a perfectly reasonable thing to do.

I think we ought to understand how these things happen. The band council has to vote the surrender of the land before it can be sold. Before the vote was taken, an offer had been made by this company-an offer to pay so much, and so much down-and there seemed to be some doubt whether it would be accepted or not. According to the information given to me, a legal representative of the company, when he saw the way the vote was going, said there would be another hundred dollars paid right away if the vote was favourable. If that had been a vote in a federal election, that vote would have been invalidated, as the hon. lady knows. It seems to me that this is just another of those things which would have made the minister doubly suspicious. That happened before Christmas, if my memory serves me right_______
On a point of order, the hon. member has just made an allegation. I think he should be called upon to prove that allegation.
As a matter of fact, the allegation is not contradictory of what the hon. lady herself said.
Oh.

The hon. member is saying that this proposition was made by the company to the Indians before the vote was taken. I say the proposition was made by the Indians to the company after the vote had been taken, and that is a different thing.
Does the hon. lady say the vote was taken before they were told that as soon as the vote had been taken they would get this hundred dollars?
That is the information I have. I was not at the meeting, and neither was the hon. member.
That is not true. That is a misrepresentation.
Then will the hon. lady tell us what happened at that meeting.

Yes, I will tell you. This deal was going through, and since Christmas was at hand the Indians asked whether they could expect to have an advance. They did not get anything extra. The locatees got an advance on the sale price. There is no secret about it. The amount of money was paid by cheque to these locatees whose land was being taken over, and it was an advance on the sale. I suggest to the hon. member that having regard to the fact that the deal

No, I was not at the meeting, either and I have no documents. But, of course, there was a record made of that meeting and the hon. lady could inquire of the superintendent what the facts are. It seems to me it is very important that these facts should be established, because the information given to me-
What information and from where?

I have been given information by someone who was there-someone who was interested in the matter-and the information I have been given is that they were told before the vote was taken. It is true no money was paid before the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration vote was taken, but they were told before the vote was taken that if the surrender was approved they would get another hundred in cash right away.

Not another hundred,
an advance.
Another hundred in cash right away-not an increase in the price, of course.
What does the hon. member mean by "another hundred dollars" if he does not mean an increase in the price?
I mean a hundred dollars in cash that they would not have got.

The hon. member still insists that this deal was made before the vote was taken. Does he insist that the company offered this advance to the Indians or is his informant telling him that the Indians asked for it, which is the information I have.
I do not know who brought the subject up, but I do not think it matters.
Oh.

I do not think it matters for this reason: When a vote is being taken on a matter of this kind at a band meeting, all the Indians who are interested not necessarily being present, it is my belief that a financial consideration of that character, no matter who initiated it, is improper. Again, to use the analogy of a federal election, it does not really matter whether you go and 'ask a fellow whether he. will offer you $10 for your vote or whether he comes to offer it to you. Whatever way that happens it is wrong, and I say there seems to have been-
More of these allegations.
The hon. member can reply in his own time. I am surprised, if the supporters of the government think this is such a good transaction, that they are so worried about any criticism of it.

Well, the only person who is being insulted during this discussion, if one can call it insult, is myself. Imputations have been made concerning my motives. The hon. lady has described me in rather unparliamentary terms-I do not take exception to that, because I know the hon. lady. I have dealt with such facts as I know. I have let the hon. lady interrupt me every time she wanted to interrupt, because I did not want to represent anything which was not a fact. I want to be very clear as to what the facts are. It seems to me that when this company showed this tremendous eagerness


to get this land, and when they had their lawyer lobbying at the meeting, suspicions should have been aroused. Why were they so desperately anxious to get this land, and so concerned about giving the Indians a little money before Christmas? It seems to me there was tremendous eagerness to get this transaction through. Another thing which is hard to explain is this: why, when the surrender was made before Christmas, did it take the hon. lady until March 14 to conclude the transaction? Did she have to wait until the other people were sure they had got hydro on the hook before she would conclude it? Does the hon. lady know whether there was any agreement between the company and the hydro before she signed the agreement herself?

The answer to the last question is, no. As far as the length of time is concerned, I have already explained that we had not one but three valuations to make. The intervening time was taken up in making a thorough investigation of the situation.
Were the valuations made after the surrender?
One was made before, and the last two were made after the surrender.

I am not going to traverse this subject further but there is one other thing I intend to suggest to the hon. lady. This transaction is not completely concluded yet. I am going to propose that the minister talk to her colleagues and suggest to them that an inquiry be made to find out whether or not any understanding or agreement had been reached between the company and the hydro before this sale was completed and, if it was, I suggest that the whole matter be looked into again to make absolutely certain that there is not some redress we can still give the Indians whose trustees we are.

60.	Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and equipment, $2,010,000.
Mr. Chairman, I believe there is a decrease in this vote. Could the hon. lady say what is involved in this particular kind of construction? Is it housing?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. This vote provides for assistance in the provision of adequate housing with minimum standards for needy Indians and also for the purchase of equipment. The details are for financing, in whole or in part, the construction of 817 housing units including minimum services if required. In addition it relates to the purchase of three new automobiles and equipment such as carpenter's tools, cement mixers for use in house construction, sewing machines for homemakers' courses and similar equipment.
Are fewer houses being built this year than last?
The winter works program accounts for a part of the reduction. An additional vote was added on to last year's estimates. That accounts for the difference.
I am afraid I do not understand that at all.
We put through a supplementary estimate in the autumn after the house met in order to do some of the work ahead of time which removed the necessity for putting that amount into this year's estimates.
That still does not answer my question. Are more houses going to be built in 1961-62?

I am told that our housing program will be maintained at approximately the same level this year as last. Present plans call for the construction of 817 housing units, as I mentioned, in 87 agencies. During the fiscal year 1961-62, work was
started on these from funds provided in the supplementary estimates that were put through in November or December last.
How many houses are under construction or have been completed in this fiscal year?
The estimated number for last year was 907 units. I might add that the 907 included 80 houses to be built from funds provided by the supplementary estimates. There are 817 to be built this year.
So that there is a decline in the housing program?

No, the hon. member is confused by the construction that was started in the interval between the two years. The 907 included 80 houses for which provision was made in the estimates that went through in November or December. If we were to deduct 80 from the 907 there would have been 827 built last year, but if you were to add 80 to the 817 there would be 897 this year.

Item agreed to.
61.	Economic development-operation and maintenance, including an amount of $6,500 for grants to promote Indian agriculture, handicrafts and economic enterprises generally, $1,113,148.

As the hon. lady knows, the subject of this vote is, next to education, my favourite. Could the hon. lady produce any figures showing how many Indians are employed? I do not refer to those who have independently secured employment but to those who have gained employment as a result of the various activities of the department under the economic development program?

I believe I gave that information in my opening statement, but I will see if we have a recapitulation available. The hon. member is inquiring about figures from the commencement of the program, is he?

No, Mr. Chairman. Perhaps I had better explain what I am really trying to get at as it may save time. I want to know how many Indians are actually employed as the result of this kind of placement activity, and so on, as compared with a year ago.

We have the figures divided into two lots, urban placements and rural and seasonal placements. In 1960 there were 3,773 in rural and seasonal placements as against 2,827 in 1959. With respect to the urban placement program, 344 were permanently employed as of November 30, 1960, which is the last date we have. I have to subtract the figure from the total to get a comparison with the year before. On the basis
2364	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration of my rapid calculation, it appears that there were about 150 in this category the year before. It has just about doubled.

In a general way does the hon. lady think, notwithstanding the greater difficulty the rest of the population has in finding employment, that as a result of the activities of the placement service and the economic development program she is doing better at the present time than she did a year ago?

I think so, Mr. Chairman. As a matter of fact this is a progressive thing. Every Indian who takes a job and makes good at it paves the way for two or three more. It is a snowballing thing. As the people who make a success set an example, it is followed by others. The effects are seen not only among their fellow Indians but their success also makes the respective employers a little more amenable to the suggestion of hiring Indians.

The hon. member for Selkirk asked earlier about Grand Rapids and developments in that part of Manitoba which appear to be extremely gratifying. I should like to know about developments at the International Nickel Company at Thompson in northern Manitoba. Has the department been successful in persuading that company to employ Indians?

We have been trying, Mr. Chairman. I do not think we have been quite as successful there as we have at Grand Rapids. We are still working on it. There have been some difficulties in the way. We hope we can persuade these people to hire more and more Indians as time goes on. I can assure the hon. member that we are not falling down on the job but are keeping right after them.

Item agreed to.
62.	Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and equipment, $511,407.
What is the nature of the construction under this vote?

This provides for capital expenditures in connection with expanded and accelerated development of commercial enterprises which tend to permit the attainment by Indians of higher standards of living. For instance, it provides for the construction of freezers for storage of food products, including wild game and commercial fish; for the breaking, fencing, ditching and drainage of land; for dams and dikes; for the rehabilitating of waterfowl, and muskrats; ice houses for commercial fishing projects; vehicles used by placement officers; saw mills for cutting lumber for houses or for sale; farm machinery, tractors and conveying equipment; bulls to improve breeds of livestock; garden


tools; breeding cattle. These are all included in this item.
There is an item of $266,004. This is mainly in an expanded agricultural and commercial fisheries program, necessitating increases in the amounts provided for breaking and fencing, ice houses, livestock, which includes cattle formerly provided for under operation and maintenance of farm machinery, flooding equipment; outboard motors for commercial fisheries. They are offset by a decrease in the amount for freezers, saw mills and conveying equipment.
It is more than doubled, in fact.
Yes.

Item agreed to.
64. Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and equipment including payments under agreements to provide joint educational facilities to Indian pupils, $7,705,000.
I notice there was a small increase. Does the hon. lady think she is getting anywhere near catching up on the need for schools?
There is a small decrease.
That is really what I meant to say. The fact that there was a decrease made me wonder whether the need for schools was somewhat less than it had been?

Well, that is a pretty broad question, Mr. Chairman. We are not replacing residential schools unless it is absolutely necessary. Some of the schools which are in use are pretty ancient. There is one place I can think of where the schools were condemned and we will have to dispose of them, and other arrangements are being made. In some instances it is possible to make arrangements with nearby non-Indian schools to absorb the pupils from day schools. This we will do wherever necessary.
I should like to see us reach the stage where all Indian children were in integrated schools but, of course, for a long time there will be areas where children will require residential schools and there will be families who, because of their living habits, will be unable to look after their own children's education unless they do go into residential schools.
For the last 10 years we have been spending a great deal of money on schools.
Yes.
One assumes that for most of that period we have been trying to catch up with the backlog?
Yes.

One assumes that, since the life of these schools is more than 10 years, certainly we ought to be reaching a point when there would be a deceleration in the rate of need for schools. That is the point.

It is true that we are catching up to some extent, but there is the other side of the question and that is the tremendous population increase. As I have said on more than one occasion, and as I think I said the other day in the house, about 50 per cent of all Indians are under 16 years of age. This raises a continuing and increasing problem with regard to their education. The offsetting factor, as I have said, is the fact that more and more of them are going into integrated schools.

Mr. Chairman, the national gallery of Canada is, at this time, completing its first year of operation in its new location in the Lome building in central Ottawa.
I have been most encouraged by the extraordinary demonstration of public support for the gallery and its activities, which is evidenced by the checked attendance since the inaugural opening of the new premises on February 17, 1960. As of the closing hour last evening, February 22, the attendance was 585,188; in other words, 585,188 visitors have entered the building in that year and five days to enjoy the collections, the circulating exhibitions, the library, lectures and study seminars, which constitute the program of this living museum of art in our national capital.
I should like to point out that in addition to the attractive program of activities talcing place in Ottawa, the national gallery of
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Canada, through its division of exhibition extension services has, since I last reported, circulated 46 travelling exhibitions throughout the length and breadth of this vast country. It has also sponsored a series of lectures on art topics in many centres, from the Atlantic provinces to the west coast. I am informed that a conservative estimate of attendance at these travelling exhibition and lecture services outside of Ottawa is approximately 244,000 persons. These, together with publications, reproductions, technical and curatorial advice, are the services the national gallery provides to the Canadian public at home.
The gallery's services abroad are also activities of considerable significance and value. We have participated successfully in the thirtieth biennale of international art in Venice, Italy, and at present the national gallery, in collaboration with the national museum, is presenting a comprehensive exhibition of Canadian art in Mexico city. The combined attendance at these two events is as yet not fully reported, but it may reach a further 100,000. It will thus be seen that the public attendance at events sponsored by the national gallery, at home and abroad, may be somewhat in excess of 900,000 persons.
In its program outlined for the coming year, the gallery proposes to extend the space devoted to Canadian works in the Lome building, it having been felt during the past year that not enough space has been available adequately to display Canadiana, particularly that of the French tradition. The north gallery, facing Albert street, formerly employed for the exposition of design centre projects, is to provide additional space for this purpose.
Among the exhibition features of the coming year will be the fourth biennale of Canadian art which will open in Ottawa on May 16, 1961. Following its exhibition in Ottawa, it will be circulated across Canada. For the first time, the trustees have declared a policy of making the biennale an open exhibition. This means that any Canadian who desires to submit work to the jury of selection may do so.
Another important exhibition will be the "Heritage de France", opening in Canada in the autumn of this year. This exhibition will bring to this country masterpieces of French painting of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. The national gallery will be one of the participating institutions in this great international project.
The curatorial division is continuing various projects on basic research; a definitive history of Canadian art, and a dictionary of national biography, dealing with Canadian artists and sculptors born before 1867, are in preparation

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration at the present time. These and many other worthy undertakings are being planned and encouraged by the board of trustees.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, the board of trustees of the national gallery of Canada have, through their careful and imaginative planning of the program of this important agency, justified the confidence and support of this committee.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to detain the committee more than about a minute, but I cannot refrain from expressing a little pardonable pride at the success that has attended the national gallery in the new building, a building which I recall seeing with my mind's eye as I looked out of my office as minister of citizenship and immigration with the architect when we discussed the site, which was visible from that office, and the planning of the building. I just wanted to recall the fact that this was one Liberal vision that became a reality. I confess that even in my wildest dreams I never thought the number of visitors to the building would be as great as in fact it has turned out to be, which would seem to suggest that there are many Canadians who genuinely believe that man does not live by bread alone. Before the estimates carry I wish to ask one or two questions, but that is all I have to say of a general nature.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest to the rather rapidly read statement of the minister on the national gallery. I hope the tempo of the reading does not indicate the minister's appreciation of the value of the gallery to Canada. I can well understand the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate's pride in the building because I think it is quite correct to say that the conception was during the previous government's tenure, and the excellence of the building and the arrangements are indicated by the very greatly increased attendance.
I have visited the gallery on a good number of occasions and, even though it is still spoken of as a temporary building, I think Canadians can view the building and its contents with pride. I have noticed Canadians and tourists from other countries going through the building who have shown a similar interest, and this is indicated by the attendance of people in the last year.
I want to pay a tribute to the director and his staff. The director is without doubt a man with ideas. He is not only a painter of distinction and a gentleman who has occupied a position with the University of Toronto but, as I was informed only recently, he has also been a military adviser to NATO. I did not know that his activities had covered such

a wide field. I was thinking about the national gallery the other day and I remembered reading the submission of the director to the royal commission on arts, letters and sciences. I may say that the present director of the gallery, Dr. Charles F. Comfort, is not only a painter but also composes with considerable cognition because I read his submission with great interest. It is very well written indeed and it is well worth anyone taking the time to read it. It has to do with painting and, as I said before, was a submission to the royal commission on arts, letters and sciences by the present director. I might say that after reading the submission I almost wished the director had taken to literature as well because we lack style in our literature and in my opinion this is a very well written article. The director has this to say:
In conclusion it may well be asked, under which system is art likely to prosper, where the state plays a part as patron, or where that function relies upon the voluntary interest and support of private institutions and individuals?
He goes on to deal with this question of magnitude and then says:
It would seem that the only valid reason for a state concern with the arts arises when it is shown that the character of local conditions endangers the preservation and development of the cultural heritage. In a small industrialized modern state, the task of supporting adequate cultural activities has far outstripped the capacity of private and voluntary means, a circumstance which must be well documented in the briefs submitted to the royal commission on cultural affairs. In expressing a hope that some instrument for the assistance and development of the arts may be set up in Canada, I am confident that it would play a most useful and vital part in our spiritual regeneration. But its constitution and the fruitful fulfilment Of its function depend upon a careful consideration of the dangers as Well as the advantages of such a procedure. The value of democracy rests in a respect for individual rights and individual differences which should be preserved rather than restricted or inhibited.
I think that paragraph puts very well indeed the necessity for assistance by the state in such matters as art galleries, museums and things of that nature if we are going to preserve our cultural heritage. Having made these few remarks I do want to say that certain matters have been brought to my attention and I have two bones, shall I say, to pick on behalf of a number of citizens of Ottawa, some of them of Scots ancestry, who have telephoned me. In fact, a gentleman telephoned me the other day and said he was not in the habit of calling socialists because he was a member of the Progressive Conservative party, but he wanted to bring to my attention certain things that he thought should be corrected so far as the national gallery is concerned.
First of all, I am informed, and I have to depend so far as these matters are concerned on my informants who are quite well

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
known and responsible people, that paintings and statuary worth millions of dollars are in storage in a building on Echo drive. I am told that the building is about 45 by 40 with a ceiling 20 to 25 feet high. I am told that there is also a collection of war paintings there which I am informed is valued at about $2 million.
I understand there are enough paintings in storage in this building on Echo drive to stock a good-sized art gallery and that in fact there are some paintings in storage which have been purchased in more recent years as the result of estimates passed by the house. When the minister replies I trust she will inform the house as to the value of the paintings in storage on Echo drive and possibly give us some idea of the number of paintings and pieces of statuary in storage because I promised these people I would raise this question.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, when we rose at six o'clock in order to refill our personal art galleries, I had paid a tribute to the director and his staff and had dealt briefly with the paintings in storage and with a valuable collection of war paintings that are also in storage.
Before proceeding with the remainder of my brief remarks I wish to say this. It has been a joy to go through the gallery this year not only because of the excellence of the building and of the arrangements, with the exception of one or two things which I shall mention later, but because of the interest I have noticed on the part of young people going through the building. It was not just a casual interest. I have stood there for some time on occasions and have noticed the genuine interest they were taking in the various types of pictures, a fact which indicated to me, particularly in view of the large number who have gone through the gallery- I think the minister mentioned a figure of something over half a million-the great value of the national gallery to us as a nation and the much greater value it can be with proper support, good public relations, a further increase in the number of paintings and so on, particularly in certain schools.
In the estimates this year I notice quite a modest amount for the purchase of new pictures. We support that item wholeheartedly. These are not times when we can be lavish in this respect but I think it is a good thing,
even under somewhat difficult circumstances, to indicate our interest by at least the estimate we have at the present time in purchasing pictures this year. I think I heard some reference in some place to the saying that money is required and we cannot afford, as a nation, to let the national gallery stagnate.
Before proceeding further, I want to suggest that if the pictures at present in storage cannot be hung in the national gallery they should be lent to other institutions. I presume some of them will be hung. I know the difficulties under which the director and his staff have worked this year. We cannot expect everything to be done in one year. However,
I suggest that as many as possible of these pictures be hung for people to see. As to those which cannot be hung or which possibly are not suitable to be hung in the circumstances under which they would be hung, I suggest that they be lent to other institutions because I believe these things should be seen, particularly by the young people of the country.
As to the war paintings, I know they are in a rather different class. I saw some of them years ago. They are quite large canvasses, I understand. Possibly it would be a good idea if these paintings could be taken over by the national archives and, in any event, hung so that the present and coming generations will have an opportunity to see in graphic form recorded on these canvasses what was done in the years of war.
I now come to another matter that I have been asked to mention by some of my Conservative friends. Last Wednesday I asked the minister why the picture of the Marquis of Lome was not hung in the national gallery. The minister replied that a picture by the distinguished pre-Raphaelite painter, Sir John Everett Millais, was at present hanging in the national gallery. The people who communicated with me on the telephone and otherwise have been frequent visitors to the gallery-they are Ottawa people-and have failed to see it. Some of them were in the gallery at the time of the minister's reply and they tramped off, hot foot, to see where this picture was. I might say that we found that it is technically correct to say that there is a picture of the Marquis of Lome in the national gallery, but under the circumstances, hardly one in substance. This fact is felt keenly by some of the Scotsmen in Ottawa.
In order to verify the telephone conversations I have held, I went to the gallery on Sunday. I am told in the first instance that the picture in storage is a magnificent picture about eight feet by six feet, of the marquis in highland costume, in full dress.
