Supply-Citizenship and Immigration At the present time I understand it is resting on its side, with dust on the frame, in this building I previously mentioned. I am also informed on making further inquiries that this extremely striking picture-according to my informant it is striking; I have not seen this picture-is actually owned by the Department of Public Works. I wish the minister would explain that matter. If so, it is a rather unusual set of circumstances.
We all know that the present national gallery building, namely, the Lome building, is a great improvement over our previous accommodation for the national art gallery. I think it is now quite true to say that we might even have the motto "Enjoy yourself in comfort with Comfort". I raise this point particularly because the Marquis of Lome was the founder of the national art gallery in 1880. When these people called me and talked to me about this matter I had a sketchy knowledge of the period of Canadian history during which the Marquis of Lome was governor general of this country, but I made it my business to get a few books from the library and I have been astounded at what I have discovered.
The Marquis of Lome was a man of vision, culture and great generosity. The Marquis of Lome was governor general of this country from 1878 to 1883. He was a viceroy. He was an ambassador. He was a unionist member of parliament for a Lancashire constituency. I might explain that a unionist is a Tory who recognizes the impact of industrial civilization and faces life in a more pragmatic way than did his predecessors. The Marquis of Lome was an economist. He wrote books. I found one in which he carried on a considerable correspondence with Henry George, the person who wrote on the single tax question. He was an artist. I found another book-and I draw it to the attention of the minister and the director-in which are included dozens and dozens of his sketches and drawings. They are delightful sketches and drawings. He was an author; he wrote books. Anyone who reads the two books he has written, entitled "Passages from the Past", which are more or less extensions of his diary, will be informed of the great part he played in Canadian history. He was a composer and playwright. He wrote his own plays and had them performed before audiences composed of guests numbering as many as 500. He was a diarist and he was the first governor general of Canada to, as it were, rap the knuckles of the colonial office in Great Britain with respect to its lack of understanding that Canada was a growing nation and should have her independence in certain matters.
He played a considerable part in creating understanding between the French and
[Mr. Herridge.l

British populations in Canada and defending the rights of the French-Canadian minority. He founded the royal society of literature in Canada and in 1880, as I have mentioned before, he founded the national gallery. In his diary there are two or three delightful passages which deal with the first three annual exhibitions or events that took place after the opening of the national gallery.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I go to some length to mention his qualities and great achievements. Anyone reading his books will see that he was a man of great wisdom, of powers of observation and of balance, a student of human nature and of nature.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question? Is the hon. member for Kootenay West a contemporary of the gentleman in question?
That was a sharp question.

answer.
I cannot claim to be a contemporary in time; I can, in spirit and purpose.
Wisdom is timeless, is it not?
That is more than the present Tories can say.

Naturally the building was named the Lome building after the Marquis of Lome, but "Lome building" does not mean much to many people coming to the national gallery, or to visitors and tourists. My point is this. Pictures are required when we come to glamourize history, to dramatize history and inform people of our history, of which we should be proud.
There is a painting in the gallery of the Marquis of Lome. It is about 29 inches by 40 inches and it was painted by Millais. It is a rather drab painting, showing the Marquis with a very pallid countenance. It is on display on a side wall in a side room on the second floor. As a matter of fact, you actually have to kneel to read the small inscription, which is a few inches long and very dark, which says this is a picture of the Marquis of Lome who was the founder of the national gallery. Because it is in an out of the way place and is so small, many people apparently visit the gallery and have no idea it is there.
My point is this. Just two pictures over and in close proximity to this picture of the Marquis of Lome is quite a large and posterior view of an attractive nude. I cannot say; I am not a judge, but I am told it is. It almost appears that the picture has been put there to distract attention from the painting of the Marquis of Lome. I can tell

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
the committee that I stood there for an hour on Sunday and watched people come along-
How did you make out with it?
-and not a single visitor noticed the painting of the Marquis of Lome: they all headed straight for this other picture.
You were standing in front of him.

No, I was standing to one side. On reading the books written by the Marquis, reading his history and some comments in his diaries, I do not think he would be at all flattered or complimented by being in such close proximity to a nude. In fact, I think that out of respect to his memory you ought to put kilts on her. I am speaking on behalf of people who have a sense of Canadian history and who appreciate these facts. I am speaking for many people of Scots descent, and I am sure for all Canadians who value our traditions, history and so on.
Therefore I do urge that the painting of the Marquis of Lome which is now in storage, the painting in which I am told he is shown in his full highland costume, a painting about six feet by eight feet, be placed facing the front doors on the ground floor as you enter the gallery, and that underneath there be an appropriate plaque which not only mentions that he was the founder of the national gallery but deals to some extent with the great contribution he made to Canadian development and Canadian nationhood.
I think this would be a fitting tribute to the Marquis of Lome and to his achievements. It would direct the attention of Canadians, visitors and tourists to the fact that this man, the Marquis of Lome, pictured in front of them was the person who founded the gallery. I am sure that as a result of this they would go away with a much clearer understanding of who he was, what he did and what his founding of the gallery has meant in the years since, and particularly at this time.
I think it would be most suitable to do that. In conclusion I do urge that consideration be given to using the paintings we have in storage and finding some place, possibly the archives for the war paintings. Then, a fitting tribute, such as I have described, should be paid to the Marquis of Lome and this painting hung in the appropriate place, namely facing the front entrance so that all will know who founded the national gallery of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I could answer the hon. member for Kootenay West. After his very eloquent plea on behalf
of the Marquis of Lome I am sure the director and the trustees will take the whole matter of the proper display of his portrait and such additional information as may be deemed appropriate in the circumstances into earnest consideration.
I may say, though, that it is true the national gallery does not own the portrait which is in storage, and consequently I do not believe it is available for display. An arrangement was made some years ago to store it for the Department of Public Works, and there it rests.
I am not qualified to judge the merits of the two paintings, but I am told that the one hanging in the gallery is much superior to the other. I may say in this regard that the other day the hon. member made the statement that having this one portrait on hand the gallery had gone to the expense of having the other one painted. Possibly he has found out in the meantime that this is incorrect. That painting was presented to the gallery by the artist himself in 1884.
The portrait by Millais?

Yes. With reference to paintings which are in storage, it is true that there are quite a few paintings in storage but the majority of them have now been moved to the Lome building where they have better facilities for them. They will, in time, be displayed on the rotation system which is in practice in the gallery.
The rest of the paintings will be removed just as quickly as possible, but I can assure the hon. member that this storage is a temporary arrangement and as soon as possible all these paintings will be in the gallery. It is not possible to show them all at one time. As I mentioned in my preliminary remarks, quite a few paintings are being moved around the country all the time on exhibition. Some of them are removed from the walls of the gallery, sent out on exhibition, others take their place and in that way the pictures are rotated at frequent intervals. In time, all of them will be on view. I am sure the hon. member would agree with this policy, because it adds interest for the viewer to find different paintings on view on different occasions when he visits the gallery.

I should like to make a suggestion with regard to the national gallery. We have a magnificent building of which we are all very proud and it has been named after the Marquis of Lome whose history we have heard so characteristically described by the hon. member for Kootenay West. However, Lome building does not mean a great deal to the average visitor to Ottawa and it seems to me that the building needs a sign on the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration face of it inscribed with the words "national gallery". This would in no way detract from the great fame of the former governor general of Canada and all the attributes which have been ascribed to him, for he was a genius in practically everything he undertook.
As I say, I think the average visitor passes the building without even knowing what is inside. I have met visitors to the city who have wished to visit the national gallery. I have directed them to it and told them what kind of building it was. It is easy to identify, but the difficulty is that no one knows what the Lome building stands for. I have in mind visitors from south of the border and from coast to coast of Canada. I think we should have one large sign on Elgin street with the words "national gallery" upon it. As hon. members may be aware, the national gallery in London, England, in Trafalgar Square has written on the face of it the words "national gallery". I think we should have that name on the Lome building-possibly two signs, one facing north and another facing east. Sufficient room is available, and my proposal could be carried out at little cost. I am sure Dr. Comfort would agree with me that the appearance of the name "national gallery" in large letters would add to the individuality of the building and to the stature of the institution. The national gallery is a shrine to which people from all over -the country should come in order to see the things we have stored there. I have no objection to the painting which is relegated to some old building and which, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Kootenay West, should be carried on into the new building.
I have no objection to that at all, but I think we should have a name outside the gallery, and I would like the minister to give consideration to that suggestion.

This matter is under active consideration at the present time. I agree with the hon. member, and I know the director does, too, that there should be some lettering capable of being easily distinguished, to designate the national gallery as such.

After listening to the opening remarks of the hon. lady, all of us here this evening realize we have much to be proud of in the director of our national gallery and his staff and in the national gallery itself. We also have much to be proud of in this great new building which has been discussed this afternoon. One of the things which was mentioned by the hon. lady-and. it has been mentioned before in this house-was the fact that not only do we have this wonderful gallery in Ottawa, visited by so many people, but we also have travelling exhibitions in every corner of this land whose displays have been receiving great attention.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to learn that the national gallery plans to open an enlarged French section to works of art from the province of Quebec.
I am well aware that the art school in our province has acquired a substantial reputation. I am therefore very proud to notice now that the director of our national gallery intends to open to this art a larger section. (Text):
As was mentioned by the previous speaker, this building bears the name of a distinguished Canadian governor general. As far back as 1880 the national gallery was brought into being. Sir, I remember when I was in high school-

Not quite, but almost. I remember when I was in high school visiting the home of my late aunt, Prudence Heward, of whom I think I have great reason to be proud, where the Canadian group of painters often met. I remember speaking to someone at one of those group meetings who told me that back at the time of confederation, at the corner of Wellington and Bank streets, strangers might have thought they were gazing on a stable, yet appearance belied the fact that this structure really housed the supreme court. It was topped by a skylight, and through that skylight the rays of heaven were first shed on the national gallery which consisted of one small room less than. 30 feet square. What a change we see today-a change which is incredible when we realize that 1867 is not so long ago, and that we are

a young nation. It is a change that is incredible when it would seem that of necessity many of our citizens were primarily preoccupied with the pioneering, economic considerations of a challenging young country. For this reason we are proud of our Canadian artists and of our gallery.
It has been said we can best judge a man by the company he keeps, and so perhaps we can judge a country in many ways by the art it produces and appreciates. Every great country the world over has produced great art in some form or other.
We know, in Canada, that most of the early painting was done by artists who had migrated from Europe and New England and, having brought with them their material outlook and national traditions, they painted the Canadian scene coloured by their previous life and training. Even the native born painters who followed soon turned to the ateliers of Europe for their guidance. But then came the now famous group of seven and a true Canadian art seemed to be taking form. At the dawn of the century the French impressionists turned the thoughts of the Canadian painter to the pictorial possibilities of his own land. After studying abroad, artists returned with vigour and enthusiasm to paint the subjects of their native provinces.
Yet, whether we are talking about these early movements-the group of seven and the subsequent association of the Canadian group of painters-or the new modern schools, be they impressionists or not, Canadian art has never been merely a vehicle for the expression of a narrow nationalism. While depicting Canada and the Canadian spirit it has always upheld the true traditions of a universal art. We know that our artists and the national gallery under its able director will continue in this work, for a truly Canadian art with universal application has a real and peaceful message for the world of today.
I have already made reference to the group of seven. More has been written about this group than any other aspect of Canadian culture. The time was ripe and they expressed the rising tide of a new national spirit. I believe it was Charles Comfort who said:
They had just the right blend of national idealism, crusade, lyricism, audacious enterprise, and intellectual and economic independence necessary to make the movement the success it was. At the time the group of seven was preparing for its first exhibition in May of 1920, we had become a confident young nation.
In an official statement made by the group in February of 1933, it was stated, in part, that members of the group of seven have:
-always maintained for themselves and others the right of freedom of expression, believing that
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration only in diversity of outlook will there ever be a widespread interest in the arts of this country.
So it follows that true art only flourishes when our real democratic freedoms are truly preserved. It has been said before and I repeat it here this evening:
The spark from heaven, who picks it up? The crowd, never. The individual, always.
Free individual expression in the arts must flourish best under our form of democratic government which is so keenly attuned to the finest aspirations of the individual.
We were told that the first world war was the war to end all wars. Many felt that promise to be an absolute truth. This notion even coloured the creative energies of our artists. They saw a colourful, ordered world key-noted with a feeling of peace and security.
The situation following world war II is different. There is a real danger to the freedom of the individual and the true spiritual democracy for which we in the west stand. The creative artist in Canada today reflects a very different sort of a world as compared with that reflected by artists in the decade after world war II. As one of the younger Canadian painters said before the royal commission on arts, letters and science in Montreal:
Canadian painting is Canadian only by reason of being first of all painting.
Canadian painting is increasingly appreciated abroad. The admiration of the critics was aroused, at the Wembley exhibition in 1924-25 and at the exposition of the Jeu de Paume in Paris in 1927. Today our young painters are being judged on the same footing as young painters from other lands.
It is true to say that it is in the field of painting that the Canadian arts are best known at home and abroad, although if I may digress very briefly I thing that even the painters must admit that Canadians have great reason to be proud-and perhaps I am being unfair in mentioning only two names- of our Maureen Forresters and Glenn Goulds.
To return to my main theme, I believe it is true to say that it is in the field of painting that the Canadian arts are best known at home and abroad. Our reputation in the arts is perhaps based mainly on our painting at this time. Certainly it has been most consistent in expressing a real spirit of Canadianism.
In its brief to the royal commission on arts, letters and science, 1949-51, the federation of Canadian artists recommended that:
-the whole conception of the functions of the national art gallery be so revised and extended that it shall become the dynamic center of activity in the visual arts throughout the whole of Canada's urban and rural population.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
The hon. lady under whose department the national gallery comes has pretty well guaranteed us that, under the able direction of the director, this is becoming, bit by bit, a real fact.
The gallery supports and encourages many travelling exhibitions, as in the past. Its services, as has been said, extend into every corner of the nation. While located in Ottawa, as I said before, the gallery is performing a valuable service across the breadth and width of this land. For that reason I could not resist the temptation of taking up the time of the committee while I congratulated the minister and the gallery on the magnificent task they are performing in Canada today. As my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate so aptly put it, "Not by bread alone do we exist".

After hearing that deeply lyrical tribute to Canadian arts I think we all appreciate and understand why the Prime Minister, whenever he has to make a speech relating to this field, takes the trouble to consult the hon. member for Brome-Mis-sisquoi.
It is not my intention to be lyrical at all.
The hon. gentleman could not be.

I want to know how much money has been spent on taking art exhibitions to smaller centres. I know there have been exhibits in larger centres but I am interested in communities with a population of less than 50,000. How many exhibitions went out and what is the estimate of the number of people who saw them last year? I should also like to know what are the plans for extending this service.

In reply to the hon. gentleman let me say that we do not have the figures of attendance for specific places. We have a record of the travelling exhibitions and an estimate would be that they have been viewed by about 250,000 people in all but what the number would be for each place I could not say.
I believe I can tell the hon. member where these exhibitions were held, but I may not be able to pick out the communities with a population of less than 50,000. As a matter of fact, one of the difficulties in this regard is that the gallery must be careful in sending out exhibitions to ensure that the paintings will be properly protected. These exhibitions cannot be housed in buildings which are not reasonably fireproof, nor can they be displayed under circumstances where proper protection cannot be afforded. This would be

one of the reasons why some of the smaller centres could not benefit from these displays from time to time.
Some of the places which might fall into the category about which the hon. member asks are Brantford, Peterborough and Brandon. Etobicoke, of course, is part of metropolitan Toronto; I suppose it is a separate municipality. Islington, again the same would apply there.

Perhaps the minister would let me make my point in regard to this. Over, the years the national film board has developed a type of field service that takes its offerings out to the people. It is not an excellent parallel, but they do get their films out to the ordinary people in the smaller places. They have coverage mapped out. One cannot get any conception at all from the hon. lady's estimates of the national gallery of Canada, as to the number of people who are doing this job of distributing and making exhibits. I know that in eastern Ontario a couple of art circles have been built up and I think especially of one that revolves around Queen's University into which exhibits of the national gallery can dovetail or fit. I insist-and I have got the parochial northwestern Ontario view of this-that the national gallery does not mean a thing in the main except for illustrations for history books and that sort of thing until there are exhibits in that part of the country. I should like to see some indication from the estimates that there is some plan to expand and develop those services. I do not feel too sorry for the people in Brantford or Etobicoke if they cannot get to national gallery exhibits because they can go to a good art gallery in Toronto. They can go to museums there. This does not apply to people in the hinterland, in the district areas. I cannot see why this area should not demand service. There are countless members in this house who are demanding that the C.B.C. get out and provide national television coverage for everybody in the country. The hon. member for Churchill is an example of this. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has the same feeling.
If we are to have national cultural agencies, surely they must keep before them, as we are insisting the C.B.C. does, the conception of national service. It is very hard for a musuem or gallery, oriented to Ottawa and to development here, to keep this in front of them especially when they have a magnificent plant and a big establishment. What I should like to suggest to the minister and to the director of the gallery is that fewer than one half of 1 per cent of my constituents will ever come to Ottawa. The distance is from

800 to 1,000 miles and in a situation such as this I think these cultural effects have to go to the people.
I have said this before in connection with both the museum and the art gallery and I should like to underline it again. I ask the hon. lady whether she can just indicate to us how many people in the national gallery are directly involved in what you might call field service, and what are the plans for improving and expanding it?

In answer to the last question, there are seven persons at the gallery and two in the field. I might tell the hon. member that in the current estimates we have an item which will cover charges for designing special exhibits for the exhibition extension service to cover the very point that he raises, namely that of making exhibitions available to smaller centres.
I think he was quite right in what he said. It is a matter that is getting the attention of the director and his staff, and we propose to follow this course and gradually expand the extension service to the point where these exhibits may be made available to the smaller communities to a greater extent than they have been heretofore.
I might just say to the hon. member I do not believe that you can actually compare an exhibition of paintings with the showing of films, because for one thing the handling is entirely different and display is on a different basis. Security is also on a different basis. Almost every aspect of service is different in the two fields. I am sure the hon. member would not want to place valuable paintings, particularly those which cannot be replaced, in jeopardy, as they undoubtedly would be in some centres. This is the reason why this whole field is being explored and why we are asking in the current estimates for an amount for this specific purpose.

In this matter of field service, the national film board has expanded its service by putting people out in the field to exploit the field and build up connections so that they know the people who can look after projectors and that sort of thing. They train them; they develop them. They know that right across the country there are people who are interested in developing films. If the national gallery is not prepared to do this I do not know who else can do it. If you have only two field officers in all of Canada, that is a rather petty figure to carry out this chore. I happen to know one of them personally. I know the very good work she does, but how can she possibly cope with and look after this tremendous area in other than a hit-or-miss way? It is
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration just impossible to cover all the settlers from the lakehead to the west coast, let us say, who would appreciate art exhibits. I know the Toronto art gallery, for example, tries to co-operate very much. As a matter of fact, I would suggest that the Toronto art gallery is really doing a chore in Ontario in this particular field that the national gallery should be doing.
In closing, I should like to suggest to the minister that next year a number of us from the smaller places would be delighted to hear that this phase of the gallery's activities had been boosted immensely.

Mr. Chairman, I just wish to make one or two brief comments. I think we ought to be grateful to the hon. member for Kootenay West for bringing to our attention the matters that he did tonight. This is not the first time that we are indebted to his diligent and exploring mind. I was very interested to hear what he had to say about the Marquis of Lome, though it is very difficult for a Macdonnell to be fair to the memory of a Campbell after the unfortunate incident at Glencoe, but I think we should try to be magnanimous in these matters.
I was very interested in the suggestion he made and also in the suggestion made by the hon. member for Port Arthur as to the importance of making available to the public the treasures which we have. If anyone has any doubt as to the importance which art, painting and literature should occupy in human life let us remind ourselves that that peerless leader of men, Churchill, in the midst of war, and all the other things which he was doing, found time both for writing and painting.
I should like to say one more thing with reference to the pictures of world war II which I understand are available. To those of us whose memories go back to world war I, it is always, I think, a satisfying experience to go to the Senate chamber where those fine murals recalling the first world war are available. I do not know whether we have anything similar with regard to the second world war, but I would suggest with deference that after all that was one of the great periods of our national life when life was lived at its intensest. I do suggest that there ought to be somewhere available, not 10 or 20 years from now, the best records which we have of those days which we all remember very well.

Mr. Chairman, this discussion has revolved around art. Unlike my friend from Kootenay West, I have no knowledge of nudes; I know very little about the Marquis of Lome. Perhaps what I am about

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration to say may be slightly out of the purview of the debate. If it is, I ask for indulgence. The wisdom of the ages, sir-and the hon. member for Greenwood touched on this in his reference to that great Englishman, Sir Winston Churchill and his paintings and writings. The wisdom of the ages is before us in words, and I am deeply concerned with the creation of a real national library. Mr. Chairman, I am sorry I did not hear the remarks of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the hon. member for Kootenay West and perhaps I may refer to matters they have already raised. I also regret very much that I did not hear the earlier part of the speech of the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi.
It is not very often that I have occasion to quarrel with the hon. member for Greenwood either philosphically or with respect to the very profound and valuable contributions he makes to the house, but I am afraid we part company on the subject of the murals in the Senate. I have the greatest respect for those persons, the hon. member particularly, who served in the first world war. Several of my uncles are buried in France as a result of that conflict. I understand that the murals in the other place are the result of the generosity of a wealthy Canadian and I sometimes find myself wondering whether what goes on in the other place is perhaps essentially none of our business in the House of Commons. However, occasionally our duty requires us to visit there, and I must confess that I am deeply unimpressed by the particular art form to be seen there.
I understand that these murals were painted and presented immediately after the first world war and the further coincidence of the burning of the parliament buildings. I do not know whether it is the business of the minister or the gallery, but I should like to offer the suggestion that consideration might be given to having something in the form of murals in the other place that would be more representative of Canada. Canada existed before the first world war and has


continued to exist since. Great events have occurred in every area of our national life, and to devote the entire space there simply to murals of the first world war seems to me, quite apart from my own artistic evaluation of them, something that might be reconsidered. Procedures in the other place are not the most mobile in the world and if we start now, perhaps by the time some of us are old enough to qualify, something may have happened in the interval.
I am concerned about the national gallery.
I had occasion to visit the gallery last session during the noon hour in response to the notices which are sent to members, for which I personally am very grateful. I was impressed with the calibre and standard of the Van Gogh exhibit particularly, but there is something that has always concerned me about the gallery. I refer to the hours that the gallery is open. The population of Ottawa is made up largely of civil servants and those whose activities relate in a very important way to the civil service. If we are to stay within the framework of an eight hour day, it seems to me some consideration should be given to shortening the hours the gallery is open during the early part of the day and extending the time for viewing in the evening.
As far as the people of Ottawa are concerned, by opening the gallery when people go to work and having it closed when people are free to go and visit the gallery it seems to me that in a sense we are defeating the purpose of the gallery. I suggest that some consideration be given to staggering the hours so that people generally in Ottawa will be able to visit the gallery in the evening.
In the township of North York, in my constituency, exhibitions are held at the North York library from time to time. I participated in the opening of one exhibition which was a one man show by Fred Varley. This grand old man of Canadian art was there in person, and as full of life and personality as his paintings. In connection with the exhibition, films of the life of Varley made by the national film board were shown in another part of the library building.
I have suggested in the house before that particularly when the house is not sitting, films such as "The Sceptre and the Mace" should be shown in the parliament buildings on a continuous basis for the benefit of tourists. It seems to me this is something that might be done at the national gallery as well and if it were combined with evening shows at the gallery couples with their children could spend a few hours not only viewing the paintings on display but also finds films related to the exhibits. The national film board has some excellent films dealing

with all of the members of the group of seven and several other prominent Canadian artists since that time.
I am suggesting two things, that we think about changing the hours and also combining films with the exhibits. I do not think it would take too much imagination to bring this about.
I am sure there are documentary films available from other countries, and again I am thinking of the Van Gogh exhibit. There must be films available dealing with his life that could be obtained and used. It seems to me the most important thing is to take full advantage of the national gallery and to have it open for a longer period during the evening.
I asked this delicate question last year and it was not answered. I hope I do a little better this year. I should like to know two things. I should like to know how the restaurant is doing in terms of profit or loss. I have never managed to eat there but I have been in the area on two occasions during the noon hour and the restaurant seemed to be well filled. If it is not doing too well, as I suspect it is not, I wonder whether any thought has been given to reconsidering the original director's suggestion that there should be a cocktail lounge in connection with the restaurant. I understand from some of my friends in this restaurant business that one way to guarantee putting the operation on a profitable basis, and improving the quality of food, is to combine a cocktail lounge with the restaurant. I should like the minister to enlighten me on these aspects of the situation.

Before the minister speaks, I should like to make one or two comments which will save her making an extra speech. In the first place, I am sorry the hon. member for Kootenay West is temporarily absent from the chamber because I wanted to take the strongest possible exception to his definition of a unionist. He does not seem to realize that unionists were Liberals, and the extraordinary definition that he conjured out of the air tonight was not really one of his major contributions to history but rather, I would say, to fancy.
I should also like to tell the hon. member for York-Scarborough that once before there was a politician who suggested that those first world war murals be taken out of the Senate and he is no longer in public life.
While I am not seeking to go into any of the circumstances and to ask the hon. lady to take action in connection with them because what has happened has happened, I want to express my very great regret at the resignation and severance of his connection with the national gallery of Mr. Donald Buchanan. Mr. Donald Buchanan, in my opinion, has contributed as much to the development of the appreciation of the arts
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration as has any living Canadian, bar none. Prior to that time, in his connection with the C.B.C., he did more than did any other single person to develop the Canadian tradition of controversial broadcasting on a fair and reasonable basis. That is another thing that I think was worked out almost uniquely in this country, almost before it was worked out anywhere else. He happens to be an old personal friend but I am not saying this on that account. To me, he is one of the Canadians who has made a contribution to our cultural life that is almost unique. I hope that he, having severed his connection with the gallery, does not intend to sever his connection with Canada and that he will find some other useful field into which he can direct his great energies and his sensitive appreciation of those things which I think all too many of us do not appreciate enough.
I should also like to make one observation -and perhaps the minister would like to extend this a bit-about what the hon. member for Port Arthur said. I happen to be one of those Canadians who, quite a long time ago now, first became interested in Canadian pictures not because of what was done by the art gallery of Toronto or by any other institution but because of the wonderful reproductions which over the years have been made available to the Canadian public at extremely low cost indeed, and which have been promoted fairly actively by the national gallery. Although it is true that there are grave difficulties and no one should underestimate them; we have seen what happens to pictures even in the art gallery of Toronto and in some other places, for example recently in Vancouver. The safety of the originals must be the first consideration because these pictures are extremely valuable. However, by the use of reproductions and, as the hon. member for York-Scarborough said a moment ago, by the use of films and that sort of thing, there is a possibility of doing something. Seeing reproductions is not as good, I admit, as being able to see the originals but it is a fairly good substitute; for the beginner, I think in many ways it is almost better than the original. This kind of service can be made available, in the case of reproductions, to any place that has a post office and in the case of films, to any place in which electricity in any of its varied forms of production can be made available.
Finally, may I say that I think it would be useful if the hon. lady would clear up all this mass of rumour that has been going on for the last six months or so about whether the new empire builder in the government, namely the Minister of Trade and Commerce,

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration has gobbled up the design centre and has pushed the hon. lady out into the cold. I think it is about time that the government came clean and told parliament just what the score is, who is responsible for the design centre, and who must argue for it before treasury board. I have no doubt whatever that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, if he even has his toe in the door, will take all the credit. But if the hon. lady has the responsibility, I would rather see her get it, I may say quite frankly.
I thought I understood her to say that the north gallery, the one facing Albert street and formerly employed for the exposition of design projects, was to provide additional space for paintings. Therefore, we should like to know where the exhibits of the design centre are going to be.

First of all, I should like to say that we all regret, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has said, that Mr. Buchanan has severed his connection with the gallery. We agree with everything he has said in that regard. However, Mr. Buchanan has chosen to live in Europe and to continue his interest in creative writing. We hope that this will not be a permanent separation from Canada, but it is a matter of his own choice and something over which we have no control.
With reference to the industrial design centre, may I say this? It is true that it has been transferred from the national gallery to the Department of Trade and Commerce, where I understand it will be set up under slightly different circumstances, but that is a matter for the Minister of Trade and Commerce to explain to the house.
I should like to tell the hon. member for York-Scarborough that the national gallery is open every day except Christmas day. It is open each day from ten o'clock a.m. to six o'clock p.m. On Tuesdays it is open right through until ten o'clock p.m. Films are shown in the theatre there every Saturday and on some Tuesday evenings. The extension of these services, of course, is dependent to a large degree on the utilization of the service and on the funds which we can acquire for an expansion program.

I should like to go back to this problem which the hon. member for Port Arthur raised. If we are going to have a national gallery, it must be very much national in interest. I certainly appreciate the opinion of the hon. lady that sending originals to small places is a great risk indeed. In fact, I know of one librarian who loses a great deal of sleep when one of these exhibits turns up at his particular establishment. It is a tremendous responsibility and the problems of fire and theft are very great indeed. I wonder

whether the answer does not lie in what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate suggested. The printing processes today are getting better than they were in the past. I think you get a clarity and depth and colour through these printing processes which are almost as accurate as the originals. Possibly you could send exhibitions of these prints throughout Canada. I think we can only really gain an appreciation of art perhaps at a very early stage in our development.
I wonder whether the minister would think over the possibilities of gathering together kits of paintings-for instance of the Kane paintings, Canadian historical paintings or renaissance paintings and sending them to schools. Perhaps this has already been started. I know the prints which are on sale at the national gallery are excellent indeed. I think this is an area in which the national gallery could perhaps expand its services. I am sure that it would receive the support of a great many members of this house who represent smaller centres. With these few remarks I think I should like to place my vote-and possibly join the hon. member for York-Scarborough in political oblivion-against those murals in the Senate as well.
Mr. Chairman, art is something about which I know absolutely nothing. Therefore I must speak on it.
Go right ahead.

When I say that, I do not say it in any boastful manner at all. I am sorry that I just happen to be one of those individuals who, in music are tone deaf and for whom art does not do anything at all, even though I have visited some of the finest art galleries of the world. I know that I am one of the few who are just not affected by art and who do not understand it. However, the majority enjoy it. Therefore I certainly want to add my words to those of other hon. members with regard to the possibility of getting more of the benefits of the national gallery to far more of the people of Canada. I think it is a shame that we should have valuable paintings in storage when there are so many people across Canada who would like to see them and to enjoy them. I say they will. My greatest experience with an art gallery was in connection with the Vancouver art gallery at the time of the sit-down strike, when they put us out of there with tear-gas bombs. Maybe that is why I am not too fond of art.
Art made you cry?
Art really made me cry that day, and I don't mean maybe.

Apparently it did not
hurt you.

It did not hurt me at all when it came to getting votes, if that is what you mean. The main reason for these remarks, Mr. Chairman, is the information we have received that the pictures of the first world war are still in storage.
It was a great experience for me a year and a half ago in Australia when I visited their most famous war memorials. We found that in the cities of Melbourne and Canberra the major attraction to the people living in those cities, and to visitors, was the war memorials and the fact that they were built around a graphic study of pictures showing what the first world war was actually like and what the conditions actually were.
The reaction of the young people in particular, when they saw these pictures of what their fathers and relatives had to go through at that time not only gave them a thirst for knowledge of the first world war and of their ancestors, but it also illustrated to them the horrors of war and gave them the determination that we must not have another one.
I have not, of course, seen these pictures which are in storage in Ottawa, but after hearing the comments in Canberra and Melbourne I think it would be not only in the interests of education in art and history, but an indication that we should not repeat in the future something that happened in the past. I am sure this would be the reaction if these paintings were assembled and put on display on a basis similar to that in Australia. They would be an education in art, history and in the horrors of war. I certainly hope that if this has not been thought of in the past by the minister and the director of the national art gallery that they will now give some thought to it. There is a threefold value to be gained by this type of picture of the first world war.

Mr. Chairman, I invite the hon. member for Vancouver East to visit the sixth floor of the national gallery, where the paintings of the first world war are on continuous exhibition and are being rotated all the time.
We have more of these paintings than we can hang at one time. There is a continuous exhibition on the sixth floor of the national gallery.

I know, but my idea was to have all these pictures properly planned and on display at all times, as they are in Melbourne. People take the entire day just going around from one picture to the other, and it is a real education.

I am sorry; we have not the space to do that.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the remarks of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate concerning political oblivion I should just like to make this comment, that if after some of the speeches I have heard him make in this House of Commons he did not commit himself to political oblivion years ago, I am not too worried about the remarks I made concerning the Senate.
This occurred to me on reflection after the minister's reply. There was another world war and we all profoundly hope it will turn out to be the last world war, with the emphasis on the "last". If the Senate is somehow wedded to this warlike atmosphere perhaps some thought might be given to the gallery commissioning some artists who still have vivid recollections of the last world war. I refer to people like Hindman and others who were commissioned by the services during the war to paint some murals. These might alternate on the walls of the Senate. They seem to spend money doing some odd things over there. I have noticed that they seem to be involved in painting their names on the ceiling of the foyer. This is an interesting occupation, but I think this idea of commissioning artists to paint second world war scenes might be considered.
With regard to the minister's reply concerning the hours of opening of the national gallery, if I understood her correctly it works out to one evening a week, Tuesday. I think this is a good thing. I was not aware of this. In view of the fact that the house is sitting and most of us are here, perhaps we would not get an opportunity to go over there on Tuesday evenings. It might be a good thing to extend the hours of opening to at least one more evening. The minister also mentioned that films are shown on Saturday afternoons. I would suggest that these films be also shown during the evening sessions.
As I mentioned in my previous remarks, I did not receive an answer last year to my question about the restaurant. I am serious in this regard. I should like to know the financial situation of the restaurant, whether it is making or losing money. I should also like to know what is the position with regard to Alan Jarvis' idea of a cocktail lounge. I did not receive an answer to these questions last year or this evening.

I did overlook the question of the restaurant when I replied to the hon. member. But this is not the responsibility of the gallery; it is a concession which is handled between the Department of Public Works and the Canadian National Institute for the Blind.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the minister will welcome this general discussion in support of this particular vote. A nation is possibly, in this secular world of ours, more often characterized by contemporaries by achievement in the industrial, commercial and secular fields, but not always in the judgment of history. In connection with those things of the spirit, heart and mind a nation is likely to be judged with more cogency than by any other form of endeavour.
By our interest in art, music, education and in these general areas of intellectual activity, we will be possibly judged in the future more than by our material achievements. Therefore I think it is well that when the inspiration comes we should join in expressing our views, immature obviously as some of them have been thus far, on these matters that have such great significance.
When I speak of immaturity of course I do not in this particular have in mind the minister herself. I do not wish anyone to think that because the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and I are associated in support of the same political ideology we are fully in accord with all aspects of our national life. I do not wish to assert that in this particular he does not enjoy preeminence over me both in terms of experience and authority. But I should like it to be known that he is not the only one in this party-and I say this by way of no reflection on him and his attainments-who is interested in this matter.
I have never claimed to be the only egghead.

My hon. friend says he is not the only egghead, and I would be the last to claim that distinction. I simply wish him to know-and I say this in the friendliest manner to a colleague-that there are others who have their views about the desirability of furthering an interest in Canadian painting and Canadian culture.
We all recognize the hon. gentleman to be pre-eminent in that field. I do not want him to think I am in any way taking away from his grandeur or the high priority that he has in that regard. I agree with him, however, in what he said about Mr. Donald Buchanan. Mr. Buchanan, was a contemporary of mine at the university. That gentleman has made a contribution, first of all to the gallery, to the design centre, and of course through his writings-his two books -particularly to Canadian painting and to an appreciation of art itself. His books on Morrice and on Canadian painting stamp him as a man of very great cultivation. I


would hope that his sojourn outside the country at this time may be temporary, so that he may return to Canada and continue the contribution which undoubtedly, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has said, he has made to this country and to Canadian painting, and to the appreciation of art generally.
He is not, of course, the only one who has made a contribution. I think we should in this national forum, this national parliament, recognize the contributions made by some other Canadians. It is dangerous to mention any Canadian in particular for fear of overlooking others who have also made contributions. However I think it is proper to remember the interest taken by the former governor general, Mr. Massey, both as a director of the national gallery and as one who has the direction of the Massey foundation. The accomplishments of Hart House and the rich contribution which Hart House has made to Canadian painting are largely the result of his imagination and initiative.
There are others like Mr. John Macauley of Winnipeg, one of the notable collectors, I believe of painting in Canada-not only Canadian paintings, but the works of some of the acknowledged masters. Mr. Macauley's service as a director of the national gallery was, I think, a distinguished contribution in this field. I think it deserves to be mentioned.
Is.

He is still a director? I am glad to know that. I thought he had retired about a year ago. I am sure the director of the gallery and the minister would acknowledge at once the contribution he has made and continues to make. There are others like the late Mr. Southam, Mr. Percy Fell and many others who, perhaps, unnoticed by many of us have added to our enrichment by their interest and by their unselfish devotion to the direction of the national gallery. I agree with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate-and I seem increasingly more to establish the fact that I am more in agreement with him than in disagreement- I agree with him that the reproduction of some of the Canadian paintings, in particular those which have been distributed throughout our libraries, throughout our schools, and right in this building in the offices of many members of parliament serve a most desirable purpose.
By the way, I think we owe to the late Mr. Claxton much of the inspiration for the distribution of these reproductions. I well remember first going into Mr. Claxton's home in Montreal about 20 years ago and seeing there, I think, the strongest collection of Canadian paintings I had ever seen in any

one home, except, possibly in that of Canada's former governor general. Mr. Claxton took a great interest in Canadian painting. This was only one facet of his great life. He, in his way, inspired many people to appreciate the value of the work of Canadian artists.
The value of these reproductions, however, lies not only in their quality, but in bringing to many thousands of people in this country who are denied the opportunity of visiting galleries, either provincial or national, an acquaintanceship with some of the work of many of our Canadian artists whose original paintings are to be found in the national gallery or in some of the provincial galleries. I well remember once visiting Mr. Henderson in Qu'Appelle, one of those Canadian artists who has perhaps done as much as any other western artist in portraying, particularly, the Qu'Appelle valley and, possibly, to a lesser extent the prairies. I believe three of his paintings are now to be found in the national gallery. I remember his telling me how much he appreciated the initiative taken by Mr. Claxton in seeing to it that two of his paintings were reproduced. He showed me one of them, and the satisfaction which was visible on Mr. Henderson's face justifies my recounting this incident tonight in the hope that this work of reproduction will be continued.
As I say, the value is not so much in the quality of the reproduction, as in that it affords to many Canadians an opportunity of seeing something of these works. This suggests to my mind that there is a strong argument not only for providing reproductions of valuable Canadian paintings, but for seeing to it that there are also reproductions of other paintings. Painting, like poetry, is something which has a national touch about it. But surely, also, it is something which extends across national boundaries. The Canadian interest in painting should not be confined to Canadian painting. It should extend to the works of all artists-the men and women great and small, who have put the consequences of their imagination on canvas-the great painters, the great classicists.
These works, too, should be appreciated and known, and the opportunity for doing so should be afforded. These, too, should be seen by Canadians. I would hope that the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver East might be acted upon, perhaps to a greater extent than is now the case. It may be difficult to provide for mobile exhibitions of some particular paintings, but it should not be difficult to provide for Canadians to see in their local galleries some of the paintings we have here in the national gallery. I do not know what the technical

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration difficulties are, but we now have springing up in Canada in many communities, where a decade ago there were no local galleries at all, galleries and strong local groups themselves engaged in painting and in encouraging the establishment and maintenance of local galleries. I have in mind, for instance, my own community, the city of Windsor, an industrial city, where we have at Willistead, an art gallery in the Willistead library-a very fine local gallery. I should like to pay tribute tonight to the men and women connected with that gallery who have done so much to acquaint the citizens of my city and my county with the value of Canadian painting and of painting generally.
The other day I attended an exhibition in that gallery, an exhibition of paintings executed by citizens of Essex county. It was indeed a revelation to me, as I am sure it was to many others. I suggest to the minister and the director that there is a magnificent opportunity to demonstrate not only to Canadians in my part of the country, but to citizens of the United States across the Detroit river, the high standard of Canadian painting, through exhibiting Canadian works of art in the Willistead gallery.
In the city of Detroit there is a very fine municipal gallery, the Detroit institute of arts, but as one who frequents that gallery from time to time, I cannot recall that there are any Canadian paintings displayed there. I am sure that if the Willistead gallery were adequately stocked with Canadian paintings these would be viewed not only by Canadians living on the Canadian side but by people from the United States living across the Detroit river. The admirable work being done by the Detroit institute of arts could be supplemented by the work of the Willistead gallery, in the sense I have indicated, by providing an increased opportunity of exhibiting Canadian paintings in the Willistead gallery.

I sat here while the hon. gentleman spoke, wondering if the hon. gentleman's latest canonization has gone to his head because he was waxing so eloquent, especially when he was defending his colleague the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
I was highly impressed by the remarks made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate when he opened the debate. The hon. gentleman started off on a very high and esoteric plane and the debate was carried on in this vein by the hon. member for Kootenay West. I thought it was simply remarkable.
The hon. gentleman started off by saying that he was most impressed by this wonderful new building which houses the national art gallery, the Lome building. He explained how he looked out of his office and envisaged the genius of the architects who had brought forth this magnificent new structure which was going to go down in history as a monument to the Liberal regime which got the vision.
I continued to listen the hon. member for Kootenay West who gave a very graphic description which held us all entranced. It was then revealed that the new building is going to be occupied by the national art gallery only temporarily and the actual national art gallery is going to be located somewhere else. At that moment the vision began to fade and grow dim.
The hon. gentleman then went on to say that the building was named after the Marquis of Lome, a former governor general. On the basis of his description it might well have been named after the marquis of forlorn because this magificent new building is to become very forlorn when the art gallery is moved and placed somewhere else. We have learned that the national gallery is going to be moved and it will also be forlorn in its new location because apparently it is going to be put out where no one will go out and visit it.
One interesting fact that came to light during the debate was that attendance at the national gallery has been simply phenomenal, that the attendance grew from practically nothing to an astounding figure. 1 believe the obvious explanation is that the national gallery is now located in the right place. It is easily accessible and many people are able to visit it.
Before too long others will probably have a vision of the new art gallery which they will put on paper so all of us can see it. I hope they will bear in mind the fact that the building should be centrally located so that it will be readily accessible.
The hon. member for Fort William was also very forlorn because the present national

art gallery does not have a sign. As I listened to the hon. member I could not help but wonder what was the matter with the people in the sign business in Ottawa. I wondered why they had not got busy long ago and sold a sign to the national art gallery to identify it.
The hon. member said that he is forlorn because no one is going to visit the gallery. Who are we to believe? We have been told by one hon. member that the attendance has been magnificent and outstanding and could not have been better, and by another member that no one attended.
The hon. member for Kootenay West went on to say that instead of looking at the magnificent picture of the Marquis of Lome the people moved over to examine a picture of a nude. The hon. gentleman was not standing in front of the picture of the Marquis but to the side. I suppose he was trying to get a side view of the nude.
This brought to my mind the fact that in the thirties Esquire magazine published some highly amusing cartoons. I recall seeing one depicting three paintings in an art gallery which told a story somewhat the reverse of the one told by the hon. member. One painting was of a nude, one was a somewhat dismal and flat landscape and the third was a rather dull still-life with flowers, and fruit on a plate. Where do you think the crowd had gathered? They had gathered in front of the landscape, and apparently the nude did not interest them at all. Apparently remarkable things happen in art galleries. However, I should like to say that the remarks made by the hon. member for Port Arthur and the hon. members for Peterborough and Scarborough were apropos. The hon. member for Vancouver East made a pertinent point which should be taken into consideration. With respect to the pictures in the Senate, the only reason I can give for their being there is that probably that is the only place large enough to hang them. Now that we have a new gallery perhaps we will find a place for them.
Let us get back to the matter of the art gallery. Mention was made tonight of how Canadian art came to life in the 1920's. It really came to the notice of the people of Canada because the artists of that day, called the magnificent group of seven, transmitted to canvas the rugged vigorous nature of Canada that no one else had been able to capture or surpass. They will go down in history. Some day you will find their paintings in the United States galleries and in other galleries throughout the world, and eventually those paintings will become highly valued and much wanted in the world's great art galleries. The only trouble is there will not

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration be enough of them to go around. If there are not enough to go around, we can supply them with the abstract art or modern art.
On every occasion that I get an opportunity I visit the Toronto art gallery. They come up with some wonderful exhibits. Recently they had an exhibition of pictures by John Sargent. They also have some wonderful pictures on exhibition painted by Hals, Raeburn, Rembrandt and Van Dyck. Afterwards I went around and looked into the other rooms of the gallery where they have those abstracts. Of course, I am sure that the national gallery here has in its basement or someplace else carloads of these things that they would like to have taken away to the dump if they could get somebody to do it. Well, I generally have a look at these abstract canvases. I think it was Sir Winston Churchill who said when he was going to paint: "Think of an innocent, nice, beautiful piece of canvas that is going to suffer the desecration that we people put on it!" I look at these abstracts and I see what mental aberrations have been transmitted to canvas. Sometimes I wonder whether they have been smoking marijuana cigarettes or whether they have given themselves a jab in the arm with cocaine, or whether it is just mental torment or the remains of delirium tremens that they put on canvas. There they are. You make your decision, and then to get a lift you go back to the art gallery and look at the beautiful pictures that have come down from the middle ages, and you say to yourself, "What wonderful artists they were". Then we have to put up with this tripe called modern art that we see on the walls of art galleries.
After listening to what was said by the minister and by the hon. member for Bon-avista-Twillingate, I thought what a wonderful picture we have now. We have the right building in the right place. We have the right director at the right time in the right place. Then I realized that it was only an illusion that we have not the right building in the right place. We have some other kind of building in the right place, but we do have the right director at the right time and we have to be thankful for that. I am going to leave this with hon. members tonight because I get tired trying to figure out the position of the members of the Liberal party. They argue between themselves as to who is going to get the honour for the emanation of this magnificent building, the admiration of the Liberal party. In the future we will get a good national gallery for the city of Ottawa, and it will be the vision of the Conservative party as usual.

I should like to make a few brief remarks on this particular vote, Mr. Chairman. I have enjoyed the debate so far this


evening. I should like to congratulate the director of the National Art Gallery and his staff on the excellent work they are doing in their fine new building. It has been my privilege in a few moments that I have had to spare from time to time to visit this gallery, and I hope to do so more frequently in the future.
I should like to add to the remarks made by the hon. members for York-Scarborough and Port Arthur regarding war paintings of world war II. I believe we have a very fair number of these in our railway committee room in the parliament buildings. Great contributions in this field were made during world war II by the present director of the national gallery, Dr. Comfort, and people such as Mr. Will Ogilvy, Carl Schaeffer, and other prominent Canadian artists.
I was rather amazed at the self-admiration society we had here this evening on the other side of the house, and I refer particularly to the hon. members for Bonavista-Twillingate and Essex East. I felt that the hon. member for Essex East was rather crowding his way into the artistic sun, so to speak, staking out a piece of territory there, perhaps in jealous admiration of his predecessor the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate rising from his seat.
Quite true.

We were surprised to hear the member for Essex East grant pre-eminence in the artistic field, as I believe he did, to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. This sort of admission is rare in this house, for pre-eminence in any field to be granted to someone else by the hon. member for Essex East.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member is under a misapprehension. He is now speaking on vote No. 253 which was passed some time ago. I thought No. 254 had been passed but we are wandering back to it again.
No. I wanted to speak on 254, the purchase account, which we are now on.
I thought the hon. member was talking on the other one.
The hon. member was just being as relevant as the rest of us.
Don't insult him.
Briefly, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member referred to individuals as intellectual precursors. There are many precursors to intellect, including fish, so I am told-
Quite right.

-but perhaps we can go into that at length at some other time. I am interested in this vote because, to be frank, the amount of money has fluctuated greatly from year to year. I am very glad to see that the amount has been increased by $50,000 for 1961-62. In our national gallery we must have in my opinion paintings brought to Canada from many parts of the world, frequently at great cost. We must have paintings old and new from many countries as well as paintings from our own Canadian artists.
I think it is perhaps just as well that the national gallery does not buy on the basis of the sort of criticism or personal preference that may often be expressed in the House of Commons. In my view that is probably a healthy situation. We all have our personal ideas as to what we like in art, and our ideas in this field are probably as varied or even more so than in the field of politics.
I should like to remark that I hope the gallery is collecting representative works of young Canadian artists as widely as possible. I know they do this to some extent but I have heard some slight criticism in the past that certain groups of our prominent young artists may perhaps have been overlooked. I think our collections in this field should be truly representative as these young artists mature.
I am sure the gallery is also following another method which to a degree might be expanded. I have in mind keeping close track of our young Canadian artists so as to know where they are and what they are doing. Perhaps they might be catalogued to some extent so that they might be better represented in exhibitions in this country and abroad, and also from the point of view of purchases by buyers from other countries. These young artists will be the greatest force in this field in Canada in the future and I think it is of paramount importance that the national gallery continue its work of collecting the best examples of their work and perhaps offer them even more encouragement in this direction.

251. Administration, production and distribution of films and other visual materials, $4,988,112.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the minister most sincerely for calling the estimates of the national film board at this time. I only have a few words to say to the charming lady who happens to be the minister responsible for the film board and they will be words of praise for the work done by the board. I wish to congratulate the chairman and members of the board and its employees for the work they are doing.
The national film board was once described by an older friend of mine who also happens to be an old friend of the member for Russell-I refer to the mayor of Ottawa, Miss Charlotte Whitton-as the most important medium of communication and information. The purpose of the board is and has been ever since its creation to make Canada better known to the Canadian people and to contribute to the projection of Canada abroad. I am happy to say that the board has discharged its responsibilities very well and deserves our appreciation.
The national film board has been granted a well deserved citizenship award and the board quite rightly is exhibiting the national citizenship award in the entrance lobby of its headquarters in St. Laurent which happens to be in my constituency. This award speaks for itself.
With regard to the purpose of making Canada better known to the Canadian people, I was very much impressed by what I read in the annual report of the board for 1959-60. According to the report, the board completed
2384	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration during the fiscal year 1959-60 353 film productions. Furthermore, in promoting the use of Canadian films by groups of all kinds the board has put 10,182 prints of its films into circulation in Canada. Films produced by the board were distributed to the Canadian people, to people of other lands, to community organizations of all kinds, to commercial theatres and television stations.
As in previous years several films produced by the board were awarded prizes by various countries throughout the world, including France, Italy, Spain, Germany, Switzerland and the United States. In 1958 the minister asked parliament to vote an additional amount of money for the production of films in foreign languages. We as members of parliament cannot place too much emphasis on the importance of such productions if we are to give other nations of the world a proper projection of Canada and the Canadian people. In order that peoples of other lands who cannot understand either of the two official languages of Canada will receive our message, we should make available to them films produced by the national film board in their own languages. Having that in mind, Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the hon. lady three questions. I should like to know how much money the board is spending in foreign language versions, what the board will be spending in the next year and what is its present stock of foreign language versions of its films.
Before resuming my seat I should like to remind the board that we shall soon be celebrating the centennial of confederation in 1867. It is my opinion that the board should start working on the production of films relating to our history so that they may be ready in 1967 to show in Canada and abroad.
(Translation):
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like the national film board to be in a position to produce films, as of now, as a preliminary to the confederation centennial celebration.
The national film board could relate the history of two peoples who have united and worked in harmony in the past. Even if there were conflicts between them at times, both made Canada the great country we know now.
Canada's history, though brief, is none the less rich and the national film board could derive its inspiration from it to produce films which would make our country better known. Canadians as well as other people could benefit from such films.

Perhaps with the indulgence of the committee I could answer those


three questions asked by the hon. member. This year $120,690 will be spent on foreign language versions. That is an increase in the appropriation of $30,000 over last year. I wonder whether I could make this suggestion to the house leader. In view of the fact that it now seems to be necessary for the Minister of Labour to inspire questions from his supporters in order to make explanations of his department, may I suggest that the government go ahead and call the labour estimates tomorrow so that we can debate these things in the house in a proper way.
May I ask the indulgence of the house to inquire what the business will be for tomorrow?

In reply to the leader of the opposition, may I say that the business of the house tomorrow is a continuation of the debate of the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. After that, we will take up the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. I know that my hon. friend the house leader has usually given a forecast of the business of the house next week, although there have been some criticisms of that procedure. If the house would like me to indicate, as a forecast only but a probable forecast, what will happen next week, I will do so. On Monday we will continue with the budget resolutions of the Minister of Finance on which the house has spent some little time already and I assume that we shall be able to conclude this business some time during Monday. Then we will go on with the resolution on today's order paper dealing with the O.E.C.D. Then we shall take the pensions bill assuming it is reported back from the committee as I understand it will be. I believe that these three items will take up Monday and Tuesday. On Wednesday we will deal with the so-called disclosure bill or the financial statistics bill which I think is the better title for it. I refer to the bill which requires

certain disclosures from corporations and unions. Then if the Department of Agriculture is not concluded tomorrow-and it will be lamentable if it is not concluded-we will go on with the Department of Agriculture estimates on Thursday and conclude with the Department of Fisheries on Friday.
There is no intention of taking the Department of Labour next week?
No.
